children.top_down_role: Gauges encouraging competition rather than joint activation within groups.

children.title: Exclusive Group Gauges
children.top_down_role: Group gauges favoring sparse selection within active groups.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Omega_{\mathrm{ex}}(x)=\left(\sum_{g\in\mathcal G}d_g\|x_g\|_1^2\right)^{1/2}
review_flags: An exclusive-lasso source with a specific locator is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the disjoint-group l1-within and l2-across exclusive norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\in\mathbb{N}\), let \(\mathcal{G}\) partition \(\{1,\ldots,p\}\) into nonempty groups, and let \(d_g>0\) for every \(g\in\mathcal{G}\). For \(x\in\mathbb{R}^p\), define \[\Omega_{\mathrm{ex}}(x)=\left(\sum_{g\in\mathcal G}d_g\|x_g\|_1^2\right)^{1/2}.\] This is a norm. Its square, \[\Omega_{\mathrm{ex}}(x)^2=\sum_{g\in\mathcal G}d_g\|x_g\|_1^2,\] is convex and can be used as a penalty. The inner \(\ell_1\) aggregation induces competition among coordinates within each group, while the outer \(\ell_2\) aggregation does not induce groupwise sparsity in the same way as an outer \(\ell_1\) aggregation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exclusive group norm uses l1 aggregation within disjoint groups and l2 aggregation across groups, thereby inducing within-group competition.
knowledge_statements.title: Exclusive Group Gauges

children.title: Within-Group Competition
children.top_down_role: Competitive activation patterns among members of a group.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial(\lambda\|x_g\|_1^2)=\{2\lambda\|x_g\|_1z:z\in\partial\|x_g\|_1\}
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports within-group competition under squared-l1 penalties; an exclusive-lasso source is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies coupling induced by the squared l1 group penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For one group \(g\) and penalty \(P_g(x_g)=\lambda\|x_g\|_1^2\) with \(\lambda>0\), \[\partial P_g(x_g)=\left\{2\lambda\|x_g\|_1z:z\in\partial\|x_g\|_1\right\}.\] Hence, when \(x_{g,j}\neq0\), every subgradient has component \(2\lambda\|x_g\|_1\operatorname{sign}(x_{g,j})\). Increasing the magnitude of any active coordinate increases \(\|x_g\|_1\) and therefore increases the marginal penalty applied to every other active coordinate in the same group. This shared marginal cost is the precise convex coupling called within-group competition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a squared-l1 group penalty, enlarging any active coefficient raises the marginal penalty on every active coefficient in that group.
knowledge_statements.title: Within-Group Competition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property content kind fits the leaf. The displayed subdifferential formula follows the convex chain rule for the squared l1 norm and correctly describes coupling among active coordinates in one group. No source or inspectable locator is supplied for either the formula or the exclusive-lasso interpretation.

children.title: Cross-Group Activation
children.top_down_role: Interactions among selections belonging to different groups.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial\!\left(\lambda\sum_g d_g\|x_g\|_1^2\right)=\prod_g 2\lambda d_g\|x_g\|_1\partial\|x_g\|_1
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports cross-group behavior of exclusive penalties; an exclusive-lasso source is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States separability and simultaneous group activation for the squared exclusive penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a partition \(\mathcal{G}\), positive weights \(d_g\), and \(P(x)=\lambda\sum_{g\in\mathcal G}d_g\|x_g\|_1^2\), the penalty is additively separable across groups: \[P(x)=\sum_{g\in\mathcal G}P_g(x_g),\qquad \partial P(x)=\prod_{g\in\mathcal G}\partial P_g(x_g).\] Consequently, activating or changing coefficients in one group does not directly change the penalty or subgradient factors of another group. Moreover, \(\partial P_g(0)=\{0\}\), so the penalty alone has no positive first-order threshold at an entirely inactive group. Thus it permits simultaneous cross-group activation while inducing competition only within each group.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The squared exclusive penalty separates across groups, so groups do not directly compete and multiple groups may activate simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Group Activation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property content kind fits the cross-group leaf. For a disjoint partition, the squared exclusive penalty and its subdifferential separate across groups, and the subdifferential of each squared-l1 term at zero is the singleton zero. The resulting activation interpretation is plausible but has no cited source or locator.

children.title: Overlap-Induced Competition
children.top_down_role: Competitive effects created by overlapping group membership.

knowledge_statements.title: Overlap-Induced Competition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Marginal competition for the overlapping exclusive-group gauge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal G\) be a finite family of possibly overlapping subsets of \(\{1,\ldots,d\}\), and define \(\Omega_{\mathcal G}(x)=\bigl(\sum_{g\in\mathcal G}\lVert x_g\rVert_1^2\bigr)^{1/2}\). If \(\Omega_{\mathcal G}(x)>0\), \(x_i\ne0\), and the sign of \(x_i\) is preserved under a positive perturbation of \(|x_i|\), then \[\frac{\partial\Omega_{\mathcal G}(x)}{\partial |x_i|}=\frac{\sum_{g\in\mathcal G:i\in g}\lVert x_g\rVert_1}{\Omega_{\mathcal G}(x)}.\] Thus an overlapping coordinate incurs the aggregate marginal contribution of every containing group, coupling its activation to coefficients in all those groups.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An overlapping coordinate contributes to every containing group, so its marginal penalty aggregates group magnitudes and creates competition across otherwise distinct groups.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\displaystyle \partial_{|x_i|}\Omega_{\mathcal G}(x)=\Omega_{\mathcal G}(x)^{-1}\sum_{g\ni i}\lVert x_g\rVert_1\).

notation.meaning: Restriction of x to coordinates in group g.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The derivative calculation is mathematically consistent with the stated overlapping exclusive-group gauge, but no inspectable source supports this gauge convention or its interpretation as overlap-induced competition.

children.title: SLOPE Sorted-l1 Family
children.top_down_role: Permutation-invariant sparsity penalties based on ordered magnitudes.

children.title: Sorted ℓ1 Penalties
children.top_down_role: Sparsity penalties indexed by ordered coefficient magnitudes.

knowledge_statements.title: Sorted ℓ1 Penalties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional ordered weighted \(\ell_1\) penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in\mathbb R^d\), let \(|x|_{(1)}\ge\cdots\ge|x|_{(d)}\) denote the coordinates' absolute values in nonincreasing order. Given weights \(\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_d\ge0\), the sorted \(\ell_1\) penalty is \[J_\lambda(x)=\sum_{j=1}^d\lambda_j|x|_{(j)}.\] It is convex and positively homogeneous. It is a norm exactly when \(\lambda_1>0\); if all weights vanish it is identically zero. Constant positive weights recover a multiple of \(\lVert x\rVert_1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sorted ℓ1 penalty weights absolute coordinates according to their magnitude rank, using nonincreasing nonnegative weights to preserve convexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(J_\lambda(x)=\sum_{j=1}^d\lambda_j|x|_{(j)}\) is convex; it is a norm iff \(\lambda_1>0\).

notation.meaning: j-th largest absolute coordinate of x.
Sorted ℓ1 penalty with weight sequence λ.

children.title: SLOPE Penalty Family
children.top_down_role: Sorted penalty models associated with SLOPE-type weighting.

knowledge_statements.title: SLOPE Penalty Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex regression estimators regularized by sorted \(\ell_1\) penalties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and let \(\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_d\ge0\). The SLOPE family consists of estimators \[\widehat\beta\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\beta\in\mathbb R^d}\left\{L(\beta)+\sum_{j=1}^d\lambda_j|\beta|_{(j)}\right\}.\] For linear regression one takes \(L(\beta)=\tfrac12\lVert y-X\beta\rVert_2^2\). The formulation is convex; existence of a minimizer additionally follows, for example, when the objective is coercive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: SLOPE minimizes a convex loss plus a sorted ℓ1 penalty, allowing larger-ranked coefficients to receive different regularization weights.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\beta\in\arg\min_\beta\{L(\beta)+J_\lambda(\beta)\}\) defines a convex estimator family.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The convex-loss-plus-sorted-l1 formulation is coherent, but a source is needed to substantiate calling the full arbitrary-convex-loss class the SLOPE family rather than a generalized SLOPE formulation.

children.title: Weight-Sequence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Geometric behavior induced by different ordered weight profiles.

knowledge_statements.title: Weight-Sequence Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity and limiting regimes of sorted \(\ell_1\) weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(J_\lambda(x)=\sum_{j=1}^d\lambda_j|x|_{(j)}\), nonnegative nonincreasing weights \(\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_d\ge0\) yield a convex permutation- and sign-invariant gauge. If \(\lambda_1=\cdots=\lambda_d=c>0\), then \(J_\lambda=c\lVert x\rVert_1\). If \(\lambda_1>0\) and \(\lambda_2=\cdots=\lambda_d=0\), then \(J_\lambda=\lambda_1\lVert x\rVert_\infty\). Strictly decreasing positive weights distinguish successive magnitude ranks while retaining normhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonincreasing nonnegative weights ensure convexity; constant weights give ℓ1, a single positive leading weight gives ℓ∞, and decreasing positive weights distinguish ranks.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(J_\lambda\) interpolates between weighted rank-sensitive norms, including \(c\lVert\cdot\rVert_1\) and \(\lambda_1\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct consequences of the sorted l1 definition
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weight regimes and l1/l-infinity specializations follow correctly from the definition, but the record has no inspectable citation.

children.title: Tied-Magnitude Geometry
children.top_down_role: Facial structure associated with equal ordered magnitudes.

knowledge_statements.title: Tied-Magnitude Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetry of sorted-penalty faces at tied magnitudes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J_\lambda\) be a sorted \(\ell_1\) penalty and let \(Q\) be any signed permutation matrix. Then \(J_\lambda(Qx)=J_\lambda(x)\) and \(\partial J_\lambda(Qx)=Q\partial J_\lambda(x)\). Consequently, if coordinates of \(x\) have tied absolute magnitudes and \(Qx=x\) permutes only within their tie blocks, then \[\partial J_\lambda(x)=Q\partial J_\lambda(x).\] Thus the exposed-face and subgradient geometry is invariant under permutations inside each tied-magnitude block; individual coordinate ranks become set-valued at a tie.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At equal absolute magnitudes, sorted penalties cannot distinguish permutations within the tied block; their subgradient and exposed-face geometry inherit that symmetry.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Qx=x\Longrightarrow \partial J_\lambda(x)=Q\partial J_\lambda(x)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: symmetry and convex subdifferential equivariance
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Signed-permutation invariance and subdifferential equivariance are correctly stated, and the property fits the tied-magnitude geometry leaf, but no source locator is provided.

children.title: k-Support-Norm Models
children.top_down_role: Convex hull models combining sparsity and Euclidean magnitude control.

knowledge_statements.title: k-Support-Norm Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex hull relaxation of simultaneous sparsity and Euclidean control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an integer \(1\le k\le d\), define \(S_k=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:\lVert x\rVert_0\le k,\ \lVert x\rVert_2\le1\}\). The \(k\)-support norm is the gauge of its convex hull: \[\lVert x\rVert_{\mathrm{sp},k}=\inf\{t>0:x\in t\,\operatorname{conv}(S_k)\}.\] Hence its unit ball is exactly \(\operatorname{conv}(S_k)\). The endpoint identities are \(\lVert x\rVert_{\mathrm{sp},1}=\lVert x\rVert_1\) and \(\lVert x\rVert_{\mathrm{sp},d}=\lVert x\rVert_2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The k-support norm has as its unit ball the convex hull of k-sparse vectors whose Euclidean norm is at most one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x:\lVert x\rVert_{\mathrm{sp},k}\le1\}=\operatorname{conv}(S_k)\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean unit ball restricted to k-sparse vectors.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard convex-hull definition of the k-support norm
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The convex-hull definition and l1/l2 endpoint identities are standard and correctly scoped, but no supporting citation with a locator is supplied.

children.title: Cardinality-Interpolating Norm Family
children.top_down_role: Cardinality-aware norm families with ordered-coordinate geometry.

children.title: Box-Norm Models
children.top_down_role: Low-complexity models based on box-constrained norm geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Box-Norm Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variational box norm with bounded coordinate scales.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(0<a\le b\) and \(c\in[da,db]\), and set \(\Theta_{a,b,c}=\{\theta\in[a,b]^d:\sum_{i=1}^d\theta_i=c\}\). The box norm is \[\lVert x\rVert_{\mathrm{box}(a,b,c)}=\left(\inf_{\theta\in\Theta_{a,b,c}}\sum_{i=1}^d\frac{x_i^2}{\theta_i}\right)^{1/2},\qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.\] It is a norm because the scale set is nonempty, compact, convex, and bounded away from zero. Models using this regularizer distribute a constrained scale budget among coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The box norm minimizes a diagonally weighted quadratic magnitude over coordinate scales constrained to a bounded box and a fixed total budget.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\displaystyle \lVert x\rVert_{\mathrm{box}(a,b,c)}^2=\inf_{\theta\in\Theta_{a,b,c}}\sum_i x_i^2/\theta_i\).

notation.meaning: Lower scale, upper scale, and total scale budget.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard variational definition of the box norm
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The variational definition is coherent for the stated nonempty scale set, but the box-norm parameterization and norm claim require an inspectable source.

children.title: Top-k Norm Models
children.top_down_role: Norm models governed by the largest ordered coordinates.

knowledge_statements.title: Top-k Norm Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Top-\(k\) Euclidean norm and its dual regularizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in\mathbb R^d\) and an integer \(1\le k\le d\), define the top-\(k\) Euclidean norm by \[\lVert x\rVert_{(k),2}=\left(\sum_{j=1}^k|x|_{(j)}^2\right)^{1/2}.\] Its dual norm is the \(k\)-support norm: \[\lVert y\rVert_{(k),2}^*=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_{(k),2}\le1}\langle x,y\rangle=\lVert y\rVert_{\mathrm{sp},k}.\] Equivalently, the unit ball of the dual norm is the convex hull of the \(k\)-sparse Euclidean unit ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The top-k Euclidean norm measures the k largest coordinate magnitudes, and its dual norm is the k-support norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert\cdot\rVert_{(k),2}^*=\lVert\cdot\rVert_{\mathrm{sp},k}\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean norm of the k largest absolute coordinates.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard top-k and k-support norm duality

children.title: Cardinality Interpolation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Parameter regimes interpolating among cardinality-sensitive geometries.

knowledge_statements.title: Cardinality Interpolation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotone interpolation of \(k\)-support unit balls and norms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For integers \(1\le k<\ell\le d\), let \(S_k=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:\lVert x\rVert_0\le k,\ \lVert x\rVert_2\le1\}\). Then \(S_k\subseteq S_\ell\), and therefore \[\operatorname{conv}(S_k)\subseteq\operatorname{conv}(S_\ell),\qquad \lVert x\rVert_{\mathrm{sp},k}\ge\lVert x\rVert_{\mathrm{sp},\ell}\quad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb R^d.\] Thus increasing the integer cardinality parameter enlarges the unit ball and weakens the norm across the discrete family, from \(\lVert x\rVert_{\mathrm{sp},1}=\lVert x\rVert_1\) to \(\lVert x\rVert_{\mathrm{sp},d}=\lVert x\rVert_2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Increasing the integer k enlarges the k-support unit ball and decreases the norm across the discrete family, from l1 at k=1 to l2 at k=d.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert x\rVert_{\mathrm{sp},k}\ge\lVert x\rVert_{\mathrm{sp},\ell}\), with \(\lVert x\rVert_{\mathrm{sp},1}=\lVert x\rVert_1\) and \(\lVert x\rVert_{\mathrm{sp},d}=\lVert x\rVert_2\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean unit ball restricted to vectors with at most k nonzero coordinates.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: unit-ball inclusion and gauge monotonicity

children.title: Parameter-Limit Geometry
children.top_down_role: Limiting norm shapes arising at extreme parameter values.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-Limit Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Endpoint and limiting geometry of the box-norm family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the box norm with \(0<a\le b\) and \(da\le c\le db\), the endpoint budgets force uniform scales: \[\lVert x\rVert_{\mathrm{box}(a,b,da)}=a^{-1/2}\lVert x\rVert_2,\qquad \lVert x\rVert_{\mathrm{box}(a,b,db)}=b^{-1/2}\lVert x\rVert_2.\] Under the extended-value convention \(x_i^2/0=0\) when \(x_i=0\) and \(+\infty\) otherwise, the boundary choice \(a=0\), \(b=1\), and integer \(c=k\) yields the \(k\)-support norm. Hence box-norm balls connect scaled Euclidean balls to cardinality-sensitive convex hulls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extreme scale budgets give scaled Euclidean norms, while the zero-lower-bound, unit-upper-bound, integer-budget limit gives the k-support norm.
assumptions_latex: \(0<a\le b\) and \(da\le c\le db\), except in the stated boundary limit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert\cdot\rVert_{\mathrm{box}(0,1,k)}=\lVert\cdot\rVert_{\mathrm{sp},k}\) under the extended-value convention.

notation.meaning: Integer cardinality budget in the boundary model.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The endpoint calculations are direct, but the identification of the extended boundary case \(\mathrm{box}(0,1,k)\) with the k-support norm depends on a convention and parameterization that require a specific source.

children.title: Sparse-Model Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Modeling failures arising from dictionary, support, and convexification mismatch.

children.title: Correlated Dictionary Atoms
children.top_down_role: Ambiguity and unstable selection under strongly aligned atoms.

knowledge_statements.title: Correlated Dictionary Atoms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifiability failure caused by duplicate or nearly aligned atoms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=[d_1,\ldots,d_p]\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}\). If \(d_i=d_j\) for distinct indices \(i\ne j\), then for every scalar \(t\), \[D(te_i)=D(te_j)=td_i,\qquad \lVert te_i\rVert_1=\lVert te_j\rVert_1=|t|.\] Hence any objective whose dependence on \(\alpha\) is only through \(D\alpha\) and \(\lVert\alpha\rVert_1\) assigns the same value to \(te_i\) and \(te_j\). In particular, if either vector is a minimizer, both are minimizers, so its selected coefficient support is not unique. Near-collinearity need not cause exact nonuniqueness but can make support selection sensitive to perturbations and noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Duplicate atoms give distinct coefficient supports with the same synthesized signal and l1 penalty; if one is optimal, the other is also optimal. Nearly duplicate atoms can make support selection unstable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(te_i\ne te_j\) for \(t\ne0\), while \(D(te_i)=D(te_j)\) and \(\lVert te_i\rVert_1=\lVert te_j\rVert_1\).

notation.meaning: i-th standard coordinate vector in coefficient space.

children.title: Analysis–Synthesis Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Divergence between coefficient sparsity and transformed-response sparsity.

knowledge_statements.title: Analysis–Synthesis Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete redundant-dictionary separation between synthesis and analysis sparsity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=[1\;1]\in\mathbb R^{1\times2}\) and use its Moore–Penrose inverse \(D^\dagger=\tfrac12(1,1)^\mathsf T\) as the canonical analysis operator. For every nonzero \(x\in\mathbb R\), \[x=D(x,0)^\mathsf T,\qquad \lVert(x,0)\rVert_0=1,\] whereas \[D^\dagger x=(x/2,x/2)^\mathsf T,\qquad \lVert D^\dagger x\rVert_0=2.\] Thus a signal admitting a one-sparse synthesis representation can have a dense canonical analysis representation; coefficient sparsity and transformed-response sparsity are not equivalent for redundant dictionaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a redundant two-copy dictionary, every nonzero scalar has a one-sparse synthesis representation but a two-nonzero canonical analysis representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{\alpha:D\alpha=x}\lVert\alpha\rVert_0=1<2=\lVert D^\dagger x\rVert_0\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The explicit pseudoinverse calculation is correct and demonstrates a genuine separation between one-sparse synthesis coefficients and the chosen canonical analysis coefficients. A source is still needed for the canonical-analysis convention and the broader analysis–synthesis interpretation.

children.title: Group-Specification Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Bias caused by incorrect, incomplete, or excessively overlapping structural groups.

knowledge_statements.title: Group-Specification Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure mechanisms for a direct overlapping-group penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For groups \(\mathcal G\subseteq 2^{\{1,\ldots,p\}}\) and weights \(w_G>0\), let \(\Omega_{\mathcal G}(x)=\sum_{G\in\mathcal G}w_G\lVert x_G\rVert_2\). If a coordinate \(j\) belongs to no group, then \(\Omega_{\mathcal G}(t e_j)=0\) for every \(t\), so the penalty provides no control in that direction. Repetition or excessive overlap instead overpenalizes shared coordinates: with two copies of \(\{1\}\), both of unit weight, \(\Omega_{\mathcal G}(t)=2|t|\), and the minimizer of \(\frac12(y-t)^2+\lambda\Omega_{\mathcal G}(t)\) is \(\operatorname{sign}(y)(|y|-2\lambda)_+\). Thus misspecified groups can respectively remove regularization or double shrinkage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uncovered coordinates escape regularization, while duplicated or excessive groups multiply penalties and shrinkage, demonstrating bias caused solely by group misspecification.
assumptions_latex: The penalty is the direct sum of group Euclidean norms, with repeated groups counted separately.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[j\notin\bigcup_{G\in\mathcal G}G\Rightarrow\Omega_{\mathcal G}(t e_j)=0,\qquad \mathcal G=(\{1\},\{1\})\Rightarrow \widehat t=\operatorname{sign}(y)(|y|-2\lambda)_+.\]

notation.meaning: restriction of x to coordinates in G

review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports the direct overlapping-group mismatch examples.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits, but no source supports the examples. Moreover, a set of groups cannot contain two copies of the same group; the formulation must use an indexed family or multiset before the duplication example is valid.

children.title: Sparse Shrinkage Bias
children.top_down_role: Magnitude distortion induced by convex sparsity penalties.

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Shrinkage Bias
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact magnitude bias of scalar soft thresholding under an orthogonal design.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(y\in\mathbb R^p\) and \(\lambda>0\), the unique minimizer of \(\frac12\lVert y-x\rVert_2^2+\lambda\lVert x\rVert_1\) is coordinatewise soft thresholding, \(\widehat x_i=\operatorname{sign}(y_i)(|y_i|-\lambda)_+\). Hence every retained coordinate satisfies \(|\widehat x_i|=|y_i|-\lambda\), so its magnitude is biased toward zero by exactly \(\lambda\). Every coordinate with \(|y_i|\leq\lambda\) is set to zero. The bias persists for arbitrarily large nonzero coordinates unless a subsequent debiasing or refitting step is used.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In orthogonal least squares, lasso soft-thresholds each retained coefficient by exactly the regularization level and deletes coefficients below that level.
assumptions_latex: The quadratic data term has identity design.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\widehat x_i=\operatorname{sign}(y_i)(|y_i|-\lambda)_+,\qquad |y_i|>\lambda\Rightarrow |y_i|-|\widehat x_i|=\lambda.\]
review_flags: No supplied locator specifically addresses soft-thresholding or lasso shrinkage bias.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The orthogonal-design soft-thresholding statement is precise and the property kind fits, but no citation with an inspectable locator supports it.

children.title: Rectangular Rank-One Atoms
children.top_down_role: Rank-one atoms for general rectangular matrices.

knowledge_statements.title: Rectangular Rank-One Atoms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Atomic description of the rectangular nuclear-norm unit ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(m,n\geq1\), define the rectangular rank-one atomic set \(\mathcal A_{m,n}=\{uv^{\mathsf T}:u\in\mathbb R^m,\ v\in\mathbb R^n,\ \lVert u\rVert_2=\lVert v\rVert_2=1\}\). Its atomic gauge is \(\gamma_{\mathcal A}(X)=\inf\{\sum_{k=1}^r c_k:X=\sum_{k=1}^r c_k u_kv_k^{\mathsf T},\ c_k\geq0,\ u_kv_k^{\mathsf T}\in\mathcal A_{m,n}\}\). Because signs may be absorbed into either factor, the set is centrally symmetric, and \(\gamma_{\mathcal A}(X)=\lVert X\rVert_*\). Consequently, \(\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A_{m,n})\) is the nuclear-norm unit ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unit-norm rectangular rank-one outer products are the atoms whose convex hull and atomic gauge give the nuclear-norm ball and nuclear norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\gamma_{\mathcal A}(X)=\lVert X\rVert_*,\qquad \operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A_{m,n})=\{X:\lVert X\rVert_*\leq1\}.\]

notation.meaning: atomic gauge generated by the atom set

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetric Rank-One Atoms

knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Semidefinite Rank-One Atoms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unsigned rank-one atoms generating the positive-semidefinite trace gauge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \(\mathbb S^n\), let \(\mathcal A_+=\{uu^{\mathsf T}:u\in\mathbb R^n,\ \lVert u\rVert_2=1\}\). Spectral decomposition gives \(\gamma_{\mathcal A_+}(X)=\operatorname{tr}(X)\) for \(X\succeq0\), and \(+\infty\) otherwise. Its unit sublevel set is \(\{X\succeq0:\operatorname{tr}(X)\leq1\}\).

children.title: Minimum Nuclear-Norm Recovery

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum Nuclear-Norm Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality-constrained convex relaxation for noiseless linear matrix measurements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal L:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to\mathbb R^q\) be linear and let \(b=\mathcal L(X_\star)\) be exact data. Minimum nuclear-norm recovery returns any \(\widehat X\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{X\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}}\lVert X\rVert_*\) subject to \(\mathcal L(X)=b\). The program is convex and replaces rank minimization by the nuclear norm. It exactly recovers \(X_\star\) when the solution set is the singleton \(\{X_\star\}\); equivalently, every nonzero \(H\in\ker\mathcal L\) satisfies \(\lVert X_\star+H\rVert_*>\lVert X_\star\rVert_*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Noiseless low-rank recovery minimizes nuclear norm over matrices matching the exact linear measurements; exact recovery means the true matrix is the unique minimizer.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal L:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to\mathbb R^q\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\widehat X\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\mathcal L(X)=b}\lVert X\rVert_*,\qquad \widehat X=X_\star\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \lVert X_\star+H\rVert_*>\lVert X_\star\rVert_*\ \text{for all }0\ne H\in\ker\mathcal L.\]

knowledge_statements.title: Singular-Value Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Singular-value formula and unitary invariance of the nuclear norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), let \(X=U\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_r)V^{\mathsf T}\) be a compact singular-value decomposition, where \(r=\operatorname{rank}(X)\) and \(\sigma_i>0\). The nuclear norm has the spectral representation \(\lVert X\rVert_*=\sum_{i=1}^r\sigma_i(X)\). Equivalently, it is the \(\ell_1\)-norm of the singular-value vector. For every pair of orthogonal matrices \(Q\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) and \(R\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), \(\lVert QXR\rVert_*=\lVert X\rVert_*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nuclear norm is the sum of a matrix's singular values and is unchanged by left or right orthogonal transformations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\lVert X\rVert_*=\sum_{i=1}^{\operatorname{rank}(X)}\sigma_i(X),\qquad \lVert QXR\rVert_*=\lVert X\rVert_*.\]

children.title: Semidefinite Nuclear-Norm Lifts

knowledge_statements.title: Semidefinite Nuclear-Norm Lifts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block-positive-semidefinite lift of the rectangular nuclear-norm epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(X\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), its nuclear norm admits the semidefinite lift \(\lVert X\rVert_*=\min_{W\in\mathbb S^m,\,Z\in\mathbb S^n}\frac12\bigl(\operatorname{tr}W+\operatorname{tr}Z\bigr)\) subject to \(\begin{pmatrix}W&X\\X^{\mathsf T}&Z\end{pmatrix}\succeq0\). Therefore \((X,t)\) belongs to the nuclear-norm epigraph exactly when there exist \(W\in\mathbb S^m\) and \(Z\in\mathbb S^n\) satisfying the same block positivity constraint and \(\frac12(\operatorname{tr}W+\operatorname{tr}Z)\leq t\). Setting \(t=1\) gives a lift of the nuclear-norm unit ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rectangular matrix's nuclear norm equals a trace-minimization problem over one block positive-semidefinite matrix, yielding lifts of its epigraph and unit ball.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\lVert X\rVert_*=\min_{\left(\begin{smallmatrix}W&X\\X^{\mathsf T}&Z\end{smallmatrix}\right)\succeq0}\frac{\operatorname{tr}W+\operatorname{tr}Z}{2}.\]

knowledge_statements.title: Factor-Variational Representations

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and any factor width \(k\geq\operatorname{rank}(X)\), \(\lVert X\rVert_*=\min_{U\in\mathbb R^{m\times k},\,V\in\mathbb R^{n\times k}:\,UV^{\mathsf T}=X}\frac12\bigl(\lVert U\rVert_F^2+\lVert V\rVert_F^2\bigr)\). The minimum is attained: if \(X=P\Sigma Q^{\mathsf T}\) is a compact singular-value decomposition, zero-padding \(U=P\Sigma^{1/2}\) and \(V=Q\Sigma^{1/2}\) to width \(k\) attains it. Hence a convex spectral penalty equals the optimal quadratic cost over latent low-rank factors, although optimization directly over the factors is generally nonconvex.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(X\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), nuclear and spectral norms are polar to one another:
\[\|X\|_*=\sup_{\|Y\|_2\leq 1}\langle X,Y\rangle,\qquad \|X\|_2=\sup_{\|Y\|_*\leq 1}\langle X,Y\rangle.\]

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

\[S_r:=\{X\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}:\operatorname{rank}(X)\leq r,\ \|X\|_g\leq1\},\qquad C_r:=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(S_r).\]
The associated low-rank-inducing norm is

children.title: Coherent Singular Subspaces

knowledge_statements.title: Coherent Singular Subspaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifiability under coordinatewise sampling of a low-rank rectangular matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(X=U\Sigma V^{\mathsf T}\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) of rank \(r\), define
\[\mu(U):=\frac mr\max_{1\leq i\leq m}\|U^{\mathsf T}e_i^{(m)}\|_2^2,\qquad \mu(V):=\frac nr\max_{1\leq j\leq n}\|V^{\mathsf T}e_j^{(n)}\|_2^2.\]
Large values indicate concentration on coordinate directions. At the extreme, let \(X=e_1^{(m)}(e_1^{(n)})^{\mathsf T}\). This matrix has rank \(1\) and maximal left and right coherence. If an observed index set \(\Omega\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\times\{1,\ldots,n\}\) omits \((1,1)\), then \(P_\Omega(X)=P_\Omega(0)=0\), so the observations do not identify \(X\). Thus rank alone cannot provide favorable uniform recovery guarantees under incomplete entry sampling; such guarantees require exclusion or separate handling of coordinate-concentrated matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximally coherent rank-one rectangular matrix can be supported on one entry, so samples omitting that entry cannot distinguish it from zero. Rank alone therefore cannot give favorable uniform guarantees from incomplete entry sampling.
assumptions_latex: \(m,n\geq1\), and \(X=U\Sigma V^{\mathsf T}\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has rank \(r\geq1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(X=e_1^{(m)}(e_1^{(n)})^{\mathsf T}\) and \((1,1)\notin\Omega\), then \(P_\Omega(X)=P_\Omega(0)\), so the sampled entries do not identify \(X\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bias in squared-loss denoising with nuclear-norm regularization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The unique solution of
\[\min_X\ \frac12\|X-Y\|_F^2+\lambda\|X\|_*\]
is obtained by singular-value soft thresholding:
\[\widehat X=U\operatorname{diag}((\sigma_i-\lambda)_+)V^{\mathsf T}.\]
Consequently, every singular value exceeding \(\lambda\) is attenuated by exactly \(\lambda\), and every singular value at most \(\lambda\) is removed. In particular, when \(Y\) is noiseless and nonzero, \(\lambda>0\) generally prevents exact recovery of its nonzero singular values, exhibiting the shrinkage bias of nuclear-norm regularization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nuclear-norm proximal estimation soft-thresholds singular values, subtracting the regularization level from every retained value and thereby creating systematic magnitude bias.
knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Shrinkage Bias

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The singular-value soft-thresholding formula precisely exhibits the stated shrinkage boundary and the content kind is suitable, but the proximal formula and uniqueness claim lack an inspectable citation.

children.title: Rank-Surrogate Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Regimes where nuclear-norm geometry poorly approximates the desired rank structure.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist matrices \(A,B\) with \(\operatorname{rank}(A)<\operatorname{rank}(B)\) but \(\|A\|_*>\|B\|_*\).

notation.meaning: a rank-one diagonal matrix with one large singular value
a rank-r diagonal matrix with unit singular values

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit elementary counterexample comparing rank and nuclear-norm orderings
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order mismatch between rank and nuclear norm without magnitude normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For any integer \(r\geq2\), choose \(M>r\) and matrices of dimension at least \(r\):
\[A=\operatorname{diag}(M,0,\ldots,0),\qquad B=\operatorname{diag}(\underbrace{1,\ldots,1}_{r},0,\ldots,0).\]
Then
\[\operatorname{rank}(A)=1<r=\operatorname{rank}(B),\qquad \|A\|_*=M>r=\|B\|_*.\]
Thus minimizing nuclear norm need not preserve the ordering induced by rank when singular-value magnitudes vary. Additional measurement geometry, normalization, or restricted conditions are required before the nuclear norm acts as an exact rank surrogate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rank-one matrix with one large singular value can have greater nuclear norm than a higher-rank matrix, so nuclear norm does not globally order matrices by rank.
knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Surrogate Mismatch

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The explicit diagonal counterexample is correct and fits the counterexample container, but no source or specifically located reference supports its broader rank-surrogate interpretation.

children.title: Tensor Extension Barriers
children.top_down_role: Representability and tractability obstacles beyond matrix rank.

assumptions_latex: \(T\in\mathbb Q^{n_1\times n_2\times n_3}\) is a third-order tensor with dimensions included in the input.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact computation of the tensor spectral norm, and hence of its polar tensor nuclear norm in general, is NP-hard.

notation.meaning: polar atomic nuclear norm generated by unit rank-one tensors

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-three tensors with rational entries and variable dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In the standard Turing model with rational input, the exact optimization problem
\[\|T\|_\sigma=\max_{\|x\|_2=\|y\|_2=\|z\|_2=1}|\langle T,x\otimes y\otimes z\rangle|\]
is NP-hard for general third-order tensors of variable dimensions. The polar tensor nuclear norm, defined as the gauge of the convex hull of unit-norm rank-one tensors, therefore lacks the general tractability enjoyed by matrix spectral and nuclear norms. This barrier concerns unrestricted tensor dimensions and does not exclude polynomial algorithms for fixed dimensions or specially structured tensor classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unlike matrix spectral and nuclear norms, their direct third-order tensor analogues are generally NP-hard to compute exactly when dimensions vary.
knowledge_statements.title: Tensor Extension Barriers

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The spectral-norm NP-hardness claim and the asserted hardness of the polar nuclear norm require a source specifying the computational problem, encoding, and reduction. Spectral-norm hardness alone does not justify the nuclear-norm conclusion as written.

children.title: Total-Variation Domain Models
children.top_down_role: Domain-dependent realizations of variation sparsity.

children.title: One-Dimensional Total Variation
children.top_down_role: Signal and change-point models on ordered domains.

knowledge_statements.title: One-Dimensional Total Variation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete signals on a finite ordered chain with unweighted adjacent differences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n\geq2\) be an integer and \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\mathbb R^n\). Define the first-difference operator \(D:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^{n-1}\) by \((Dx)_i=x_{i+1}-x_i\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n-1\). The one-dimensional discrete total variation is
\[\operatorname{TV}_1(x):=\|Dx\|_1=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}|x_{i+1}-x_i|.\]
It is a convex seminorm whose nullspace consists exactly of constant signals. Penalizing \(\operatorname{TV}_1(x)\) promotes sparse first differences and hence piecewise-constant signals with few change points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite signal of length at least two, one-dimensional total variation is the sum of its absolute adjacent differences. It vanishes exactly on constant signals and promotes few change points.
assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb N\) with \(n\geq2\), and \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\mathbb R^n\) has the natural linear ordering.

notation.meaning: first-difference operator for indices from 1 through n-1

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical discrete one-dimensional total-variation definition

children.title: Continuum BV Total Variation
children.top_down_role: Measure-theoretic variation models on continuous domains.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\in BV(\Omega)\) exactly when \(\operatorname{TV}(u)<\infty\), in which case \(\operatorname{TV}(u)=|Du|(\Omega)\).

notation.meaning: space of smooth compactly supported vector fields
distributional derivative of u as a vector-valued Radon measure
total-variation measure of the distributional derivative

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical dual definition of total variation and BV
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar integrable functions on an open Euclidean domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(u\in L^1(\Omega)\), define its distributional total variation by
\[\operatorname{TV}(u;\Omega):=\sup\left\{\int_\Omega u\,\operatorname{div}\varphi\,dx:\varphi\in C_c^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^d),\ \|\varphi\|_{L^\infty}\leq1\right\}.\]
The function \(u\) belongs to \(BV(\Omega)\) precisely when this quantity is finite. In that case the distributional gradient \(Du\) is a finite vector-valued Radon measure and
\[\operatorname{TV}(u;\Omega)=|Du|(\Omega).\]
For \(u\in W^{1,1}(\Omega)\), this reduces to \(\operatorname{TV}(u;\Omega)=\int_\Omega|\nabla u|\,dx\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is of bounded variation when the dual divergence supremum is finite; this value equals the mass of its distributional derivative measure.
knowledge_statements.title: Continuum BV Total Variation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dual divergence definition, BV characterization, Radon-measure identity, and W^{1,1} specialization are standard and fit the definition container, but they require an inspectable analysis reference with a specific locator.

children.title: Discrete Grid Total Variation
children.top_down_role: Finite-difference variation models on regular grids.

knowledge_statements.title: Discrete Grid Total Variation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-difference TV on a finite rectangular grid with explicitly selected neighbor edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Omega_h\subset h\mathbb{Z}^d\) be a finite rectangular grid, let \(E_h\) contain the selected unordered nearest-neighbor pairs, and let \(u:\Omega_h\to\mathbb{R}\). The edge-based discrete total variation is
\[\operatorname{TV}_h(u)=\sum_{\{p,q\}\in E_h} w_{pq}|u_q-u_p|,\]
where \(w_{pq}\ge 0\) may include grid-spacing and quadrature factors. Equivalently, after orienting every edge and forming the weighted incidence difference operator \(D_h\), one has \(\operatorname{TV}_h(u)=\|D_hu\|_1\). Boundary behavior is determined by the choice of \(E_h\); no differences leaving \(\Omega_h\) are included unless a boundary extension is specified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Discrete grid TV sums weighted absolute finite differences over selected neighboring grid points; the edge set encodes the boundary convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{TV}_h(u)=\sum_{\{p,q\}\in E_h}w_{pq}|u_q-u_p|=\|D_hu\|_1\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically coherent and fits the discrete-grid TV container, but no inspectable source or locator supports the weighting and boundary-convention formulation.

children.title: Graph Total Variation
children.top_down_role: Incidence-, cut-, and edge-based variation models on graphs.

knowledge_statements.title: Graph Total Variation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted edge-difference TV for scalar signals on a finite undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E,w)\) be a finite undirected graph with edge weights \(w_e\ge 0\), and let \(u\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\). Its graph total variation is
\[\operatorname{TV}_G(u)=\sum_{e=\{i,j\}\in E}w_e|u_i-u_j|.\]
After assigning an arbitrary orientation to the edges and defining \((Bu)_e=u_i-u_j\), this equals \(\|WBu\|_1\), where \(W=\operatorname{diag}(w_e)\). The value is independent of the chosen orientation. For an indicator \(u=\mathbf{1}_S\), it equals the weighted cut capacity \(\sum_{e\in\delta(S)}w_e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Graph TV sums weighted absolute signal jumps across edges and reduces to weighted cut capacity for a vertex-set indicator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{TV}_G(u)=\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}w_{ij}|u_i-u_j|=\|WBu\|_1\).

notation.meaning: edges crossing from S to its complement

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The edge-difference, incidence-operator, and indicator-cut statements are standard and internally consistent, but they have no cited source with a specific locator.

children.title: Local TV Geometry Variants
children.top_down_role: Alternative ways to aggregate directional, spatial, and channelwise variation.

children.title: Anisotropic Total Variation
children.top_down_role: Direction-separable local variation geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Anisotropic Total Variation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direction-separable discrete TV using the pointwise \(\ell_1\) geometry of coordinate differences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Omega_h\subset h\mathbb{Z}^d\) be finite, and let \(D_k u(p)\) denote a prescribed forward difference in coordinate direction \(k\), set to zero or omitted when its neighbor is unavailable. The anisotropic discrete total variation of \(u:\Omega_h\to\mathbb{R}\) is
\[\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{aniso}}(u)=\sum_{p\in\Omega_h}\sum_{k=1}^{d}\alpha_{p,k}|D_k u(p)|,\]
with \(\alpha_{p,k}\ge0\). Thus coordinate-direction increments are penalized separately; for unit weights the local integrand is the \(\ell_1\)-norm of the discrete gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Anisotropic TV adds absolute coordinate differences separately, giving each discrete gradient the local ℓ1 geometry.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{aniso}}(u)=\sum_{p,k}\alpha_{p,k}|D_ku(p)|\).

notation.meaning: finite difference in coordinate direction k

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The direction-separable discrete definition fits anisotropic TV, but no authoritative locator supports the selected weighted convention and boundary treatment.

children.title: Isotropic Total Variation
children.top_down_role: Rotation-coupled local variation geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Isotropic Total Variation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete scalar TV coupling coordinate differences through a pointwise Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Omega_h\subset h\mathbb{Z}^d\) be finite and define the discrete gradient \(D u(p)=(D_1u(p),\ldots,D_du(p))\), using a fixed boundary convention. The isotropic discrete total variation is
\[\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{iso}}(u)=\sum_{p\in\Omega_h}\alpha_p\|D u(p)\|_2,\]
where \(\alpha_p\ge0\). Unlike direction-separable TV, all coordinate differences at a grid point enter one Euclidean norm. With unit weights and consistently transformed differences, this local integrand is invariant under orthogonal changes of spatial coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Isotropic TV couples all coordinate differences at each grid point through one Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{iso}}(u)=\sum_{p\in\Omega_h}\alpha_p\|Du(p)\|_2\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Euclidean coupling definition fits isotropic discrete TV, but the coordinate-invariance sentence requires authoritative support and careful qualification for a fixed grid discretization.

children.title: Spatially Adaptive Directional TV
children.top_down_role: Spatially or directionally varying local variation models.

children.title: Spatially Weighted TV
children.top_down_role: Local variation models with spatially varying penalty strength.

knowledge_statements.title: Spatially Weighted TV
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted isotropic discrete TV with a prescribed nonnegative spatial weight field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Omega_h\) be a finite grid, let \(D\) be a fixed discrete gradient, and let \(a:\Omega_h\to[0,\infty)\) be prescribed independently of the optimization variable. The spatially weighted total variation is
\[\operatorname{TV}_{a}(u)=\sum_{p\in\Omega_h}a(p)\|Du(p)\|_2.\]
More generally, the Euclidean norm may be replaced by any fixed norm on the local difference vector. The functional is convex and positively homogeneous in \(u\). It is a norm modulo constants only when the positively weighted difference structure connects the grid and the chosen boundary convention removes no additional directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Spatially weighted TV multiplies each local gradient magnitude by a prescribed nonnegative location-dependent weight.
assumptions_latex: \(a\) and \(D\) are fixed with respect to \(u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{TV}_{a}(u)=\sum_pa(p)\|Du(p)\|_2\) is convex and positively homogeneous in \(u\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The prescribed-weight definition and nullspace qualification are plausible and fit the container, but no source with a specific locator supports them.

children.title: Directional TV
children.top_down_role: Variation models favoring prescribed orientation geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Directional TV
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete TV induced by prescribed local linear transformations of spatial gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D u(p)\in\mathbb{R}^d\) be the discrete gradient on a finite grid \(\Omega_h\), and let \(A_p\in\mathbb{R}^{r_p\times d}\) be prescribed matrices. Directional total variation is
\[\operatorname{TV}_{A}(u)=\sum_{p\in\Omega_h}\|A_pDu(p)\|_2.\]
The matrices may rotate, scale, or suppress selected gradient directions. For example, if \(v_p\) is a prescribed unit vector and \(A_p=\operatorname{diag}(\beta_{\parallel},\beta_{\perp})R_p\), where \(R_p\) resolves vectors parallel and perpendicular to \(v_p\), the two directional components receive distinct penalties. Fixed \(A_p\) make the functional convex in \(u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directional TV applies a prescribed local linear transform to each gradient before measuring its magnitude.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) and every \(A_p\) are fixed with respect to \(u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{TV}_{A}(u)=\sum_p\|A_pDu(p)\|_2\) is convex and positively homogeneous.

notation.meaning: dimension of the transformed local gradient

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The matrix-induced functional is a plausible directional-TV convention, but the term has multiple conventions and needs a source. The displayed two-component diagonal example also implicitly requires d=2, which is not stated.

children.title: Adaptive TV
children.top_down_role: Variation models whose local geometry responds to data or prior structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive TV
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Guide-adapted TV whose weights or directional metrics are fixed before optimizing the target image.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g\) be observed guide data, and let a specified rule produce nonnegative weights \(a_p(g)\) and matrices \(A_p(g)\). With these quantities held fixed while optimizing \(u\), define
\[\operatorname{TV}_{g}(u)=\sum_{p\in\Omega_h}a_p(g)\|A_p(g)Du(p)\|_2.\]
This is an adaptive total variation functional: local penalization changes according to the guide. It is convex in \(u\) whenever the generated weights and matrices do not subsequently depend on \(u\). If they are recomputed from the current iterate, the resulting joint or iteratively reweighted model need not be convex and is not represented by this fixed-guide definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adaptive TV derives local weights or directions from guide data, then holds them fixed to retain convexity in the reconstructed signal.
assumptions_latex: \(a_p(g)\) and \(A_p(g)\) remain fixed during optimization over \(u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{TV}_{g}(u)=\sum_pa_p(g)\|A_p(g)Du(p)\|_2\) is convex in \(u\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixed-guide construction is mathematically coherent and its convexity claim is correct under the stated independence condition, but it represents only one adaptive-TV convention and lacks an authoritative locator.

children.title: Vanishing-Weight Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Loss of structural control where local TV weights become ineffective.

knowledge_statements.title: Vanishing-Weight Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of coupling and enlarged nullspaces when TV weights vanish across an interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be the difference graph of a discrete TV functional
\[J(u)=\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}w_{ij}|u_i-u_j|,\qquad w_{ij}\ge0.\]
Delete every edge with \(w_{ij}=0\), and suppose the remaining positive-weight graph has connected components \(V_1,\ldots,V_m\) with \(m>1\). Then every signal that is constant on each \(V_k\), with possibly different constants across components, satisfies \(J(u)=0\). Consequently, vanishing weights along a separating interface remove variation coupling across that interface, enlarge the nullspace beyond global constants, and prevent coercivity modulo a single global constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weights vanishing along a separating interface disconnect the TV graph, allowing unpenalized jumps and enlarging the seminorm nullspace.
assumptions_latex: The positive-weight subgraph has \(m>1\) connected components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u|_{V_k}=c_k\) for arbitrary \(c_k\) implies \(J(u)=0\), so \(\dim\ker J\ge m\).

notation.meaning: connected components of the positive-weight graph

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary content kind is appropriate, and the disconnected positive-weight graph yields the stated enlarged nullspace, but no inspectable source supports the claim.

children.title: Vectorial Total Variation
children.top_down_role: Coupled variation models for multichannel and vector-valued data.

knowledge_statements.title: Vectorial Total Variation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Channel-coupled discrete TV using a matrix norm of the multichannel Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(u:\Omega_h\to\mathbb{R}^c\) be a multichannel signal. At each grid point \(p\), arrange its directional differences as the discrete Jacobian \(Ju(p)\in\mathbb{R}^{c\times d}\). The Frobenius-coupled vectorial total variation is
\[\operatorname{VTV}(u)=\sum_{p\in\Omega_h}\|Ju(p)\|_{F}.\]
All channels and spatial directions at a location are therefore coupled within one matrix norm. More generally, replacing \(\|\cdot\|_F\) by any fixed matrix norm gives a convex vectorial TV functional, while the particular norm determines the channel and directional coupling geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vectorial TV jointly penalizes the multichannel Jacobian at each location using a matrix norm such as the Frobenius norm.
assumptions_latex: \(u:\Omega_h\to\mathbb{R}^c\) is defined on a finite grid.
The discrete Jacobian uses a fixed boundary convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{VTV}(u)=\sum_{p\in\Omega_h}\|Ju(p)\|_F\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Frobenius-coupled definition is valid and fits vectorial TV, but it selects one of several channel-coupling conventions without an authoritative source locator.

children.title: Nonlocal Total Variation
children.top_down_role: Variation models built from nonlocal neighborhoods or similarity graphs.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonlocal Total Variation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise-difference TV over prescribed nonlocal neighborhoods or similarity weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V\) be a finite sample set, let \(w_{ij}=w_{ji}\ge0\) be prescribed similarity weights with \(w_{ii}=0\), and let \(u\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\). The nonlocal total variation is
\[\operatorname{NLTV}_{w}(u)=\frac12\sum_{i,j\in V}w_{ij}|u_i-u_j|.\]
The factor \(1/2\) prevents double counting. Weights may connect spatially distant but similar samples, so the model is local on the weighted similarity graph rather than on the physical grid. Equivalently, \(\operatorname{NLTV}_{w}\) is weighted graph total variation on edges for which \(w_{ij}>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonlocal TV sums weighted absolute differences between possibly distant samples selected by a fixed similarity graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{NLTV}_{w}(u)=\frac12\sum_{i,j}w_{ij}|u_i-u_j|\).

notation.meaning: nonlocal total variation induced by w

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The symmetric pairwise formula and its graph-TV interpretation are coherent, but the record lacks a cited nonlocal-TV source with a specific locator.

children.title: Total-Variation Formulation Family
children.top_down_role: Canonical exact, constrained, penalized, and inverse-problem interfaces for TV.

children.title: TV-Constrained Models
children.top_down_role: Estimation under an explicit variation budget.

knowledge_statements.title: TV-Constrained Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex estimation with an explicit upper bound on a chosen TV functional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space, let \(C\subseteq X\) be nonempty and convex, let \(F:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be a proper convex data-fidelity function, and let \(J:X\to[0,+\infty]\) be a convex total-variation functional. For a budget \(\tau\ge0\), the TV-constrained model is
\[\min_{u\in C} F(u)\quad\text{subject to}\quad J(u)\le\tau.\]
Its feasible set \(K_\tau=\{u\in C:J(u)\le\tau\}\) is convex. If \(F\) is lower semicontinuous, \(K_\tau\) is nonempty and compact, and \(K_\tau\cap\operatorname{dom}F\ne\varnothing\), then a minimizer exists. The parameter \(\tau\) directly bounds the admitted variation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A TV-constrained model minimizes convex data mismatch over signals whose total variation does not exceed a specified budget; a minimizer exists under lower semicontinuity, compact feasibility, and finite objective value at some feasible point.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is a convex TV functional and \(\tau\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{u\in C}\{F(u):J(u)\le\tau\}\) is a convex optimization problem.

source_refs.locator: 1.3.3 Constrained Minimization p. 50

source_witnesses.locator: 1.3.3 Constrained Minimization p. 50

children.title: TV-Penalized Models
children.top_down_role: Data-fitting models with variation regularization.

knowledge_statements.title: TV-Penalized Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex estimation balancing data fidelity against a TV regularization penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space, let \(C\subseteq X\) be nonempty and convex, let \(F:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be a proper convex data-fidelity function, and let \(J:X\to[0,+\infty]\) be a convex total-variation functional. For \(\lambda\ge0\), the TV-penalized model is
\[\min_{u\in C}\;F(u)+\lambda J(u).\]
The objective is convex. When \(\lambda>0\), larger values assign greater relative cost to variation. If the objective is lower semicontinuous and coercive on the closed set \(C\), then the minimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A TV-penalized model minimizes convex data mismatch plus a nonnegative multiple of total variation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{u\in C}\bigl(F(u)+\lambda J(u)\bigr)\) is a convex optimization problem.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The penalized convex model and conditional attainment statement are mathematically coherent and fit the container, but no authoritative TV-regularization source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: TV Denoising Models
children.top_down_role: Edge-preserving denoising using variation control.

assumptions_latex: The observation satisfies \(f\in L^2(\Omega)\), where \(\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is bounded and open.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A TV-denoised estimate is any minimizer \(u_\lambda\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in BV(\Omega)\cap L^2(\Omega)}\{\frac12\lVert u-f\rVert_{L^2(\Omega)}^2+\lambda |Du|(\Omega)\}\).

notation.meaning: Space of integrable functions with distributional derivative a finite Radon measure
Total variation of the distributional derivative of the image

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical Rudin-Osher-Fatemi convex denoising formulation
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous scalar-valued quadratic-fidelity TV denoising on a bounded domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given noisy data \(f\in L^2(\Omega)\) on a bounded open set \(\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^d\), the quadratic-fidelity total-variation denoising model is
\[
\min_{u\in BV(\Omega)\cap L^2(\Omega)}\frac12\lVert u-f\rVert_{L^2(\Omega)}^2+\lambda |Du|(\Omega),\qquad \lambda>0.
\]
The fidelity term penalizes deviation from the observation, while \(|Du|(\Omega)\) penalizes spatial variation without requiring classical differentiability. The objective is proper, convex, and strictly convex in \(u\) because of the quadratic term; consequently, whenever a minimizer exists, it is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: TV denoising balances squared error to a noisy image against its total variation, preserving sharp transitions while suppressing oscillation.
knowledge_statements.title: TV Denoising Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ROF formulation and uniqueness qualification are mathematically standard and fit the leaf, but no inspectable source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: TV Inverse-Reconstruction Models
children.top_down_role: Variation-regularized reconstruction from indirect or incomplete observations.

assumptions_latex: The data satisfy \(y\in Y\), where \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
The forward map \(A:X\to Y\) is linear, and \(\Phi(\,\cdot\,;y):Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A TV-regularized reconstruction is any \(x_\lambda\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\{\Phi(Ax;y)+\lambda\operatorname{TV}(x)\}\).

notation.meaning: Discrete or continuous total-variation regularizer appropriate to the signal domain

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical convex TV regularization for linear inverse problems
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex reconstruction with a linear forward model and general convex fidelity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:X\to Y\) model indirect, blurred, subsampled, or otherwise incomplete measurements \(y\in Y\). A penalized TV inverse-reconstruction model is
\[
\min_{x\in X}\ \Phi(Ax;y)+\lambda\operatorname{TV}(x),\qquad \lambda>0,
\]
where \(\Phi(\,\cdot\,;y)\) is a proper lower-semicontinuous convex fidelity and \(\operatorname{TV}\) is a proper lower-semicontinuous convex variation functional. Thus the reconstruction problem is convex. Existence follows, for example, when the objective is coercive or has a nonempty compact sublevel set; uniqueness requires additional strict convexity or injectivity conditions and is not guaranteed by TV alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inverse-reconstruction model fits measurements produced by a linear forward operator while penalizing the total variation of the unknown signal.
knowledge_statements.title: TV Inverse-Reconstruction Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-dimensional convex inverse-reconstruction template fits the leaf, but its formulation, convexity, existence, and uniqueness claims lack cited support with a specific locator.

children.title: TV Models with Nongaussian Fidelities
children.top_down_role: Variation regularization paired with robust, impulse-noise, or count-data fidelities.

assumptions_latex: The feasible set \(C\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
The fidelity \(\Phi(\,\cdot\,;y)\) and total variation \(\operatorname{TV}\) are proper, lower-semicontinuous, convex functions on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The estimator is any \(x_\lambda\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\{\Phi(Ax;y)+\lambda\operatorname{TV}(x)\}\), with \(\Phi\) chosen from a non-Gaussian observation model.

notation.meaning: Convex data fidelity induced by the observation model
Closed convex constraint set, such as a nonnegative orthant

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard convex likelihood-plus-TV template for non-Gaussian data
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex robust, impulse-noise, and count-data variants of the TV reconstruction template.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A non-Gaussian TV model has the form
\[
\min_{x\in C}\ \Phi(Ax;y)+\lambda\operatorname{TV}(x),\qquad \lambda>0,
\]
with a fidelity matched to the data law rather than squared error. Typical convex choices are \(\Phi(z;y)=\lVert z-y\rVert_1\) for impulsive errors and, for nonnegative count data, \(\Phi(z;y)=\sum_i(z_i-y_i\log z_i)\) on coordinates satisfying \(z_i>0\), with the convention for \(y_i=0\) given by continuity. Convexity is retained whenever \(C\), \(\Phi\), and \(\operatorname{TV}\) are convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Non-Gaussian TV models replace squared error by a convex fidelity suited to outliers, impulse noise, or count observations.
knowledge_statements.title: TV Models with Nongaussian Fidelities

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports the non-Gaussian fidelity examples. Moreover, A, X, Y, and the domain of the composed fidelity are not introduced consistently, and the Poisson example does not explicitly assume nonnegative count data and an admissible positive prediction.

children.title: Fused-Lasso Models
children.top_down_role: Joint sparsity and variation models on ordered or graph domains.

assumptions_latex: The response is \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\), the design is \(X\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), and \(G=(V,E)\) has \(|V|=n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A fused-lasso estimate is any minimizer of \(\frac12\lVert y-X\beta\rVert_2^2+\lambda_1\lVert\beta\rVert_1+\lambda_2\lVert D_G\beta\rVert_1\).

notation.meaning: Coefficient vector indexed by graph vertices
Oriented incidence matrix of the graph

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard graph fused-lasso objective, including the ordered-chain specialization
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph fused lasso, with the ordinary fused lasso obtained from a path graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an oriented graph incidence matrix \(D_G\), the fused-lasso model is
\[
\min_{\beta\in\mathbb{R}^n}\frac12\lVert y-X\beta\rVert_2^2+\lambda_1\lVert\beta\rVert_1+\lambda_2\lVert D_G\beta\rVert_1.
\]
The first penalty promotes zero coefficients, while \(\lVert D_G\beta\rVert_1=\sum_{(i,j)\in E}|\beta_i-\beta_j|\) promotes equality across adjacent vertices. For the path graph with edges \((i,i+1)\), the variation term becomes \(\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}|\beta_{i+1}-\beta_i|\). The objective is convex; setting \(\lambda_1=0\) yields graph-TV signal approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fused lasso jointly encourages sparse coefficients and equality of coefficients connected along an ordered sequence or graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Fused-Lasso Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The graph fused-lasso definition and path-graph specialization fit the leaf, but no authoritative source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Trend-Filtering Models
children.top_down_role: Discrete higher-order difference models for piecewise-polynomial structure.

assumptions_latex: Observations \(y_i\in\mathbb{R}\) occur at equally spaced ordered locations \(i=1,\ldots,n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The order-\(k\) trend-filtering estimate minimizes \(\frac12\lVert y-\beta\rVert_2^2+\lambda\lVert D^{(k+1)}\beta\rVert_1\).

notation.meaning: First-difference matrix with rows computing adjacent differences
Recursively defined difference matrix of order r
Fitted values at the ordered locations

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard equally spaced discrete trend-filtering formulation
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equally spaced univariate trend filtering with an \(\ell_1\) difference penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an integer \(k\geq0\), order-\(k\) trend filtering solves
\[
\min_{\beta\in\mathbb{R}^n}\frac12\lVert y-\beta\rVert_2^2+\lambda\lVert D^{(k+1)}\beta\rVert_1,
\]
where \(D^{(1)}\) computes adjacent differences and higher differences are formed recursively. Vanishing entries of \(D^{(k+1)}\beta\) impose the discrete relation of a polynomial sequence of degree at most \(k\); nonzero entries identify knots. Hence the fitted sequence is piecewise polynomial in the discrete sense, with adaptively selected knots. The case \(k=0\) is one-dimensional TV denoising.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Trend filtering penalizes higher-order discrete differences, producing an adaptively knotted piecewise-polynomial fitted sequence.
knowledge_statements.title: Trend-Filtering Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The intended trend-filtering model is standard, but no source is supplied. The recursive difference-operator notation suppresses changing matrix dimensions, and the necessary relation between n and k is not stated.

children.title: Higher-Order Total Variation
children.top_down_role: Variation models based on higher-order derivative structure.

assumptions_latex: The domain \(\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is open, and \(k\geq1\) is an integer.
The function \(u\in L^1(\Omega)\) has distributional derivative \(D^k u\) representable by a finite tensor-valued Radon measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The order-\(k\) total variation is \(\operatorname{TV}^k(u)=|D^k u|(\Omega)\).

notation.meaning: Total mass of the tensor-valued derivative measure
Functions with finite distributional variation of order k

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard distributional higher-order variation seminorm
convention_review: tensor norm and boundary null space should be fixed globally
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributional scalar higher-order variation using the total mass of a tensor-valued measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an integer \(k\geq1\), define
\[
BV^k(\Omega)=\{u\in L^1(\Omega):D^k u\text{ is a finite tensor-valued Radon measure}\},
\qquad
\operatorname{TV}^k(u)=|D^k u|(\Omega).
\]
Here the total mass is computed with a fixed norm on order-\(k\) tensors. The functional \(\operatorname{TV}^k\) is convex and positively homogeneous. It vanishes on polynomials of degree at most \(k-1\), subject to the distributional interpretation on \(\Omega\), so it is generally a seminorm rather than a norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Higher-order total variation measures the Radon-mass of a higher distributional derivative and favors piecewise-polynomial structure.
knowledge_statements.title: Higher-Order Total Variation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The higher-order variation definition needs an authoritative source and a fixed tensor-norm convention. On a disconnected domain, vanishing kth derivative yields a polynomial of degree at most k-1 on each connected component, so the global polynomial statement is overstated.

children.title: Infimal-Convolution TV
children.top_down_role: Latent combinations of multiple variation orders.

assumptions_latex: The functionals \(J_1,J_2:X\to[0,+\infty]\) are proper convex variation penalties on a vector space \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Their weighted infimal-convolution regularizer is \((\alpha_1J_1\square\alpha_2J_2)(u)=\inf_{u=u_1+u_2}\{\alpha_1J_1(u_1)+\alpha_2J_2(u_2)\}\).

notation.meaning: Infimal convolution of two extended-real functionals
Latent components whose sum is the modeled signal

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Latent additive decomposition combining two convex variation penalties or derivative orders.

source_refs.locator: Section 4.5, Infimal Convolution and Conjugacy, p. 102

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For proper convex variation penalties \(J_1\) and \(J_2\), their weighted infimal convolution is
\[
(\alpha_1J_1\square\alpha_2J_2)(u)
=
\inf_{u_1,u_2\in X:\,u_1+u_2=u}
\bigl\{\alpha_1J_1(u_1)+\alpha_2J_2(u_2)\bigr\}.
\]
Choosing, for example, \(J_1(u)=|Du|(\Omega)\) and \(J_2(u)=|D^2u|(\Omega)\) permits one latent component to carry first-order variation and another to carry second-order variation. The resulting functional is convex; it is not the pointwise sum of the two penalties, because the decomposition is optimized.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Infimal-convolution TV splits a signal into latent components and assigns each component the variation order that represents it most economically.
knowledge_statements.title: Infimal-Convolution TV

source_witnesses.locator: Section 4.5, Infimal Convolution and Conjugacy, p. 102

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited section supports generic infimal convolution, but the exact leaf concerns TV and mixed derivative-order specialization. That specialization and its modeling interpretation require an additional inspectable source.

children.title: Total Generalized Variation
children.top_down_role: Coupled derivative-field models for piecewise-smooth structure.

assumptions_latex: The domain \(\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is bounded and open, and \(u\in BV(\Omega)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The second-order total generalized variation is \(\operatorname{TGV}_{\alpha}^{2}(u)=\inf_{w\in BD(\Omega)}\{\alpha_1|Du-w\mathcal{L}^d|(\Omega)+\alpha_0|Ew|(\Omega)\}\).

notation.meaning: Space of vector fields with bounded symmetric deformation
Symmetrized distributional derivative of the vector field

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard second-order TGV definition with a symmetric-gradient auxiliary field
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order scalar TGV with an auxiliary bounded-deformation field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(u\in BV(\Omega)\), the second-order total generalized variation functional is
\[
\operatorname{TGV}_{\alpha}^{2}(u)
=
\inf_{w\in BD(\Omega)}
\left\{\alpha_1|Du-w\mathcal{L}^d|(\Omega)+\alpha_0|Ew|(\Omega)\right\}.
\]
The auxiliary field \(w\) approximates the first derivative of \(u\), while its symmetrized derivative \(Ew\) is separately controlled. The functional is convex and positively homogeneous. It vanishes on affine functions and can represent piecewise-affine behavior without charging a first-order variation penalty throughout every nonconstant region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Second-order TGV couples a signal derivative to an auxiliary field and penalizes both their mismatch and the field's symmetric variation.
knowledge_statements.title: Total Generalized Variation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed second-order TGV definition is standard and fits the leaf, but no authoritative source with a specific definition, theorem, section, or page locator is supplied.
