children.title: Coarea Geometry
children.top_down_role: Geometric organization of scalar variation through threshold slices.

assumptions_latex: The domain \(\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is open, and \(u\in BV(\Omega)\) is real valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The total variation decomposes as \(|Du|(\Omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}P(\{u>t\};\Omega)\,dt\).

notation.meaning: Superlevel set of u at threshold t
Relative perimeter of a measurable set in the domain

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical coarea formula for scalar BV functions
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar BV coarea formula relating variation to the geometry of superlevel sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every real-valued \(u\in BV(\Omega)\), the superlevel set \(E_t=\{x\in\Omega:u(x)>t\}\) has finite perimeter in \(\Omega\) for almost every \(t\in\mathbb{R}\), and
\[
|Du|(\Omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}P(E_t;\Omega)\,dt.
\]
Thus scalar total variation is the accumulated relative perimeter of all superlevel sets. Threshold values for which \(E_t\) lacks finite perimeter form a Lebesgue-null set and do not affect the integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The coarea formula expresses a scalar function's total variation as the integral of the perimeters of its superlevel sets.
knowledge_statements.title: Coarea Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scalar BV coarea representation is precise and appropriately classified, but the theorem-level claim lacks an authoritative citation with a specific locator.

children.title: Level-Set Perimeters
children.top_down_role: Perimeter structure associated with scalar level sets.

assumptions_latex: The set \(E\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is Lebesgue measurable, and \(\Omega	d\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is open.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The relative perimeter is \(P(E;\Omega)=|D\chi_E|(\Omega)\), and for finite-perimeter sets it equals \(\mathcal{H}^{d-1}(\partial^*E\cap\Omega)\).

notation.meaning: Indicator function of the measurable set
Reduced boundary of a finite-perimeter set

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard De Giorgi definition and representation of relative perimeter
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measure-theoretic relative perimeter used in the BV coarea formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The relative perimeter of a measurable set \(E\subset
t\mathbb{R}^d\) in an open set \(\Omega\) is
\[
P(E;\Omega)=|D\chi_E|(\Omega),
\]
provided the distributional derivative \(D\chi_E\) is a finite vector-valued Radon measure; otherwise the perimeter is \(+\infty\). For a finite-perimeter set, De Giorgi's representation gives
\[
P(E;\Omega)=\mathcal{H}^{d-1}(\partial^*E\cap\Omega),
\]
so the perimeter measures the set's measure-theoretic interface inside \(\Omega\), excluding boundary contributions lying outside the relative domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A level set's relative perimeter is the total variation of its indicator and equals the area of its reduced boundary.
knowledge_statements.title: Level-Set Perimeters

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The perimeter definition and De Giorgi representation require an authoritative source. The assumptions contain the malformed token "\td", and the statement contains an extraneous "t" before "\mathbb{R}^d".

children.title: Nested Superlevel Sets
children.top_down_role: Inclusion geometry across varying scalar thresholds.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Whenever \(s<t\), one has \(E_t\subseteq E_s\); moreover, \(u(x)=\sup\{t\in\mathbb{R}:x\in E_t\}\) at every point where \(u(x)\) is finite.

notation.meaning: Strict superlevel set at threshold t

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: immediate order property of superlevel sets
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order structure and pointwise reconstruction associated with strict superlevel sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E_t=\{x\in\Omega:u(x)>t\}\). For any thresholds \(s,t\in\mathbb{R}\) satisfying \(s<t\),
\[
E_t\subseteq E_s.
\]
Thus increasing the threshold can only remove points, and the entire superlevel family is nested. At every \(x\in\Omega\) where \(u(x)\in\mathbb{R}\), the value is recovered from this family by
\[
u(x)=\sup\{t\in\mathbb{R}:x\in E_t\}.
\]
Consequently, a collection proposed as the strict superlevel sets of one scalar function must satisfy this nesting compatibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Superlevel sets shrink monotonically as the threshold rises, and the nested family determines the original scalar function pointwise.
knowledge_statements.title: Nested Superlevel Sets

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The nesting and finite-value reconstruction properties are correct and fit the leaf, but no source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Thresholding Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Connections between scalar TV models and binary level-set problems.

assumptions_latex: The domain \(\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is open, and \(u\in BV(\Omega)\) is real valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For almost every \(t\in\mathbb{R}\), the thresholded indicator \(v_t=\chi_{\{u>t\}}\) belongs to \(BV(\Omega)\) and satisfies \(|Dv_t|(\Omega)=P(\{u>t\};\Omega)=\mathcal{H}^{d-1}(\partial^*\{u>t\}\cap\Omega)\).

notation.meaning: Binary thresholding of the scalar field
Measure-theoretic interface of the thresholded region

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite-perimeter threshold interface consequence of BV coarea theory
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measure-theoretic interfaces produced by almost-everywhere thresholding of a scalar BV function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a real-valued function \(u\in BV(\Omega)\), define the binary thresholding \(v_t=\chi_{\{u>t\}}\). For almost every \(t\in\mathbb{R}\), the set \(\{u>t\}\) has finite perimeter and
\[
|Dv_t|(\Omega)
=P(\{u>t\};\Omega)
=\mathcal{H}^{d-1}(\partial^*\{u>t\}\cap\Omega).
\]
Hence the reduced boundary of the thresholded region is its measure-theoretic interface, and its area is exactly the TV cost of the binary thresholding. Exceptional thresholds may fail to define a finite-perimeter interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Almost every threshold of a BV function produces a binary region whose TV equals the area of its measure-theoretic interface.
knowledge_statements.title: Thresholding Interfaces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The almost-everywhere finite-perimeter threshold-interface statement is a standard consequence of BV coarea theory, but it lacks an authoritative citation with a specific locator.

children.title: Continuum Dual-Field Certificates
children.top_down_role: Vector-field and calibration interfaces for continuum TV.

knowledge_statements.title: Continuum Dual-Field Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subgradient certificate for isotropic total variation on a bounded Lipschitz domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d\) be bounded and Lipschitz, and let \(u\in BV(\Omega)\cap L^2(\Omega)\). A field \(p\in L^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^d)\) certifies \(z\in\partial\operatorname{TV}(u)\) if \(\|p\|_\infty\le 1\), \(\operatorname{div}p\in L^2(\Omega)\), the normal trace satisfies \(p\cdot n=0\) on \(\partial\Omega\), and its pairing with \(Du\) obeys \((p,Du)=|Du|\) as Radon measures. Under these conditions, \[z=-\operatorname{div}p\in\partial\operatorname{TV}(u),\qquad \operatorname{TV}(v)\ge \operatorname{TV}(u)+\langle z,v-u\rangle_{L^2}\quad\text{for every }v\in BV(\Omega)\cap L^2(\Omega).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded vector field aligned with the distributional derivative and having zero boundary flux certifies a TV subgradient through its negative divergence.
assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d\) is bounded with Lipschitz boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(-\operatorname{div}p\in\partial\operatorname{TV}(u)\).

notation.meaning: Distributional derivative of u as a vector-valued Radon measure.
Pairing measure between the bounded divergence field p and Du.
Outward unit normal to the domain boundary.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind and continuum-TV scope fit the leaf, and the formulation is plausible, but the Anzellotti pairing, normal trace, and exact L2-subgradient characterization require an authoritative source with a specific locator.

children.title: Discrete Flow Certificates
children.top_down_role: Dual-flow and cut interpretations for grid and graph TV.

knowledge_statements.title: Discrete Flow Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Edge-flow optimality certificate for graph-TV denoising.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an oriented finite graph with incidence matrix \(B\), positive edge weights collected in \(W\), and \(\operatorname{TV}_G(u)=\|WBu\|_1\). A vector \(q\in\mathbb R^E\) is an admissible edge flow when \(|q_e|\le1\) and \(q_e=\operatorname{sign}((Bu)_e)\) whenever \((Bu)_e\ne0\). For data \(f\in\mathbb R^V\) and \(\lambda>0\), the vector \(u\) minimizes \(\frac12\|u-f\|_2^2+\lambda\operatorname{TV}_G(u)\) exactly when an admissible flow satisfies \[f-u=\lambda B^TWq.\] Thus the residual is certified as the weighted divergence of a capacity-bounded flow saturated across every nonzero discrete jump.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph-TV solution is certified when its residual equals the divergence of a capacity-bounded edge flow aligned with every nonzero jump.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite oriented graph and every diagonal entry of \(W\) is positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\) is optimal if and only if \(f-u=\lambda B^TWq\) for an admissible flow \(q\).

notation.meaning: Diagonal matrix of positive edge weights.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind fits the leaf and the finite-dimensional optimality condition is internally consistent, but no cited source supports the graph-TV flow characterization.

children.title: TV Discretization Failure Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Artifacts and ambiguities associated with first-order variation and its discretization.

children.title: Staircasing Artifacts
children.top_down_role: Piecewise-constant bias in smoothly varying regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Staircasing Artifacts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact one-dimensional example where TV denoising creates plateaus from affine data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\Omega=(0,1)\), consider \[\min_{u\in BV(0,1)}\frac12\int_0^1(u(x)-x)^2\,dx+\lambda |Du|(0,1).\] If \(0<\lambda\le1/8\) and \(c=\sqrt{2\lambda}\), its minimizer is \[u_\lambda(x)=\begin{cases}c,&0\le x<c,\\x,&c\le x\le1-c,\\1-c,&1-c<x\le1.\end{cases}\] Hence the strictly increasing affine datum acquires constant intervals of length \(c\) adjacent to both boundaries. This supplies a concrete staircasing mechanism: first-order TV permits derivative concentration while suppressing gradual variation on nontrivial regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One-dimensional TV denoising turns an affine ramp into a ramp with two artificial constant boundary plateaus.
assumptions_latex: The fidelity is squared \(L^2(0,1)\) distance and TV uses the natural zero-flux dual convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u_\lambda\) is constant on \([0,\sqrt{2\lambda})\) and \((1-\sqrt{2\lambda},1]\) although the datum is strictly increasing.

notation.meaning: Total variation of the distributional derivative on the interval.
Plateau length, equal to the square root of twice the regularization parameter.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample kind fits this failure-artifact leaf, but the exact ROF minimizer and parameter range require a source with a specific theorem, example, or page locator.

children.title: Variation-Shrinkage Bias Family
children.top_down_role: Attenuation associated with variation shrinkage.

children.title: Contrast Attenuation
children.top_down_role: Loss of intensity separation across reconstructed regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Contrast Attenuation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact contrast loss in the two-vertex graph-TV model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider two vertices joined by an edge of weight \(w>0\), with data \(f=(a,b)\) satisfying \(a\ge b\). The minimizer of \[\frac12(u_1-a)^2+\frac12(u_2-b)^2+\lambda w|u_1-u_2|\] has reconstructed contrast \[u_1-u_2=\max\{a-b-2\lambda w,0\}.\] Therefore every unfused solution loses exactly \(2\lambda w\) of contrast, while data contrast at most \(2\lambda w\) is removed completely by fusion. The attenuation is caused by the linear TV charge on the jump magnitude.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two connected samples, TV reduces contrast by twice the weighted regularization level and fuses contrasts below that threshold.

notation.meaning: Weight of the single graph edge.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind and two-vertex contrast formula fit the leaf and are mathematically consistent, but the record contains no inspectable citation.

children.title: Amplitude Shrinkage
children.top_down_role: Systematic reduction in recovered signal magnitudes.

knowledge_statements.title: Amplitude Shrinkage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Peak shrinkage in a two-vertex TV denoising problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For data \(f=(A,0)\) on a two-vertex graph with edge weight \(w>0\), let \(u\) minimize \[\frac12\|u-f\|_2^2+\lambda w|u_1-u_2|.\] If \(A>2\lambda w\), then \[u=(A-\lambda w,\lambda w),\] so the peak amplitude is reduced by \(\lambda w\) and the background is raised by the same amount. If \(0\le A\le2\lambda w\), then \(u=(A/2,A/2)\). Thus TV regularization systematically shrinks isolated amplitudes even without noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A two-sample impulse loses peak amplitude under TV; sufficiently small impulses are flattened completely to their mean.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u=(A-\lambda w,\lambda w)\) when \(A>2\lambda w\), and \(u=(A/2,A/2)\) otherwise.

notation.meaning: Weight of the edge joining the two vertices.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind appropriately captures amplitude shrinkage, and the piecewise minimizer is consistent with the stated objective, but no source locator is supplied.

children.title: Bias Regimes
children.top_down_role: Model settings that control the severity of variation-induced bias.

knowledge_statements.title: Bias Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Piecewise formula separating shrinkage and fusion regimes for two-region TV.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a\ge b\), \(w>0\), and \(\lambda>0\). For the two-vertex objective \[F(u)=\frac12(u_1-a)^2+\frac12(u_2-b)^2+\lambda w|u_1-u_2|,\] the unique minimizer is \[u^*=\begin{cases}(a-\lambda w,b+\lambda w),&a-b>2\lambda w,\\((a+b)/2,(a+b)/2),&a-b\le2\lambda w.\end{cases}\] The first regime preserves the edge but biases both levels toward each other; the second removes the edge entirely. The threshold \(2\lambda w\) therefore separates contrast-shrinkage and fusion bias.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two-region TV has an edge-preserving shrinkage regime above a threshold and a complete-fusion regime at or below it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The bias changes from level shrinkage to complete fusion at \(a-b=2\lambda w\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the leaf's piecewise bias-regime description, but the exact threshold and minimizer formula lack cited support.

children.title: Debiasing Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Model interfaces intended to separate structural recovery from amplitude correction.

knowledge_statements.title: Debiasing Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Least-squares refitting on the jump support selected by graph TV.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given data \(f\in\mathbb R^V\), a graph incidence matrix \(B\), and a TV estimate \(\widehat u\), define its detected jump set by \(S=\{e:(B\widehat u)_e\ne0\}\). Form the model subspace \[M_S=\{v\in\mathbb R^V:(Bv)_e=0\text{ for every }e\notin S\}.\] The support-preserving debiased estimate is \[u^{\mathrm{db}}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{v\in M_S}\frac12\|v-f\|_2^2.\] Compute it by orthogonally projecting \(f\) onto \(M_S\), and output \(u^{\mathrm{db}}\). This refit retains the selected partition while removing the linear TV penalty on its region amplitudes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After TV selects jump locations, project the data onto signals constant across all inactive edges to refit region amplitudes without TV shrinkage.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite graph with incidence matrix \(B\).
A graph-TV estimate \(\widehat u\in\mathbb R^V\) is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u^{\mathrm{db}}=P_{M_S}f\) preserves the selected inactive-edge equalities and minimizes squared error on that model.

notation.meaning: Detected set of nonzero graph differences.
Subspace determined by the selected jump support.
Orthogonal projector onto the model subspace.

children.title: Grid Metrication Bias Family
children.top_down_role: Orientation bias introduced by discrete neighborhood geometry.

children.title: Grid-Induced Anisotropy
children.top_down_role: Orientation preference introduced by discrete grid geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Grid-Induced Anisotropy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Four-neighbor discretization converges to anisotropic rather than rotationally invariant TV.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a square grid of spacing \(h\), define the axis-neighbor discrete variation of sampled smooth data by \[\operatorname{TV}_h(u)=h\sum_{i,j}\bigl(|u_{i+1,j}-u_{i,j}|+|u_{i,j+1}-u_{i,j}|\bigr).\] For \(u\in C^1(\overline\Omega)\) and consistent interior sampling, Riemann-sum convergence gives \[\operatorname{TV}_h(u)\longrightarrow\int_\Omega\bigl(|\partial_1u|+|\partial_2u|\bigr)\,dx.\] The limit uses the \(\ell^1\) norm of the gradient, not the Euclidean norm. Consequently, the four-neighbor template is intrinsically anisotropic and is not a consistent discretization of isotropic TV without further stencil design.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Axis-neighbor grid TV approaches an L1 gradient norm, so its continuum limit favors coordinate directions instead of being rotation invariant.
assumptions_latex: Samples and boundary truncation are consistent as \(h\to0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{TV}_h(u)\to\int_\Omega(|\partial_1u|+|\partial_2u|)\,dx\), generally not \(\int_\Omega|\nabla u|_2\,dx\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the anisotropy leaf, and the scaling is plausible for a rectangular grid, but the convergence claim and boundary/counting conventions need a cited source.

children.title: Metrication Artifacts
children.top_down_role: Blocky or faceted shapes induced by discrete distance structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Metrication Artifacts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Taxicab perimeter distortion produced by four-neighbor grid paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a four-neighbor square grid with unit edge costs, every path joining lattice points whose displacement is \((m,n)\in\mathbb Z^2\) has length at least \(|m|+|n|\), and a monotone path attains this value. Hence the induced grid distance is \[d_4((0,0),(m,n))=|m|+|n|,\] whereas the Euclidean distance is \(\sqrt{m^2+n^2}\). For diagonal displacement \((k,k)\), their ratio is \(\sqrt2\). Thus discrete TV boundaries and shortest contours may become axis-aligned or blocky because the stencil measures taxicab rather than Euclidean geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Four-neighbor grids measure diagonal displacement too expensively, producing blocky, axis-aligned contours and a diagonal distortion factor of square root two.
assumptions_latex: The lattice is \(\mathbb Z^2\) with horizontal and vertical unit-cost edges only.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_4((0,0),(m,n))=|m|+|n|\), with diagonal-to-Euclidean distortion \(\sqrt2\).

notation.meaning: Shortest-path distance on the four-neighbor grid.
Integer displacement between two lattice sites.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the metrication-artifact leaf, and the four-neighbor distance calculation is correct, but no source supports the connection to TV contour artifacts.

children.title: Orientation Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Dependence of reconstruction behavior on feature orientation.

knowledge_statements.title: Orientation Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Angular dependence of four-neighbor discrete perimeter density.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a straight interface with Euclidean unit normal \(n=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\), the anisotropic continuum density induced by four-neighbor TV is \[\phi_4(n)=|\cos\theta|+|\sin\theta|.\] Its value ranges from \(1\) for axis-aligned normals to \(\sqrt2\) for diagonal normals. Thus two congruent interfaces related by rotation can receive different regularization costs: \[1\le\frac{\phi_4(n)}{|n|_2}\le\sqrt2.\] This angular dependence makes edge retention, smoothing strength, and recovered contour geometry sensitive to orientation relative to the sampling grid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Four-neighbor TV charges a straight edge according to its angle, with diagonal orientations costing up to square root two times axis-aligned ones.
assumptions_latex: The discrete model uses equal horizontal and vertical nearest-neighbor weights.
The interface is locally straight with Euclidean unit normal \(n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi_4(n)=|\cos\theta|+|\sin\theta|\in[1,\sqrt2]\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean unit normal to the interface.
Angle of the interface normal relative to the first grid axis.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind fits orientation sensitivity and the angular density is consistent with four-neighbor anisotropic TV, but the claim lacks an inspectable citation.

children.title: Neighborhood-Stencil Dependence
children.top_down_role: Variation in model geometry across discrete neighborhood choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Neighborhood-Stencil Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Surface-tension formula induced by a finite weighted difference stencil.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subset\mathbb Z^2\setminus\{0\}\) be a finite symmetric stencil and let \(\alpha_k=\alpha_{-k}\ge0\). For the directional discrete variation built from differences along \(k\in K\), the associated homogeneous interfacial density has the form \[\phi_K(n)=\frac12\sum_{k\in K}\alpha_k|k\cdot n|.\] Changing \(K\) or the weights changes \(\phi_K\), hence changes the effective unit ball, perimeter, and preferred edge orientations. Finite stencils generally yield polygonal anisotropy; rotational invariance requires an appropriate limiting or enriched construction rather than arbitrary neighborhood enlargement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted finite stencil induces a specific directional surface tension, so changing neighbors or weights changes the effective perimeter geometry.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The effective interfacial density is \(\phi_K(n)=\frac12\sum_{k\in K}\alpha_k|k\cdot n|\) under the stated counting convention.

notation.meaning: Finite set of lattice displacement vectors.
Nonnegative weight assigned to displacement k.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits stencil dependence, but the density formula depends on the precise discrete energy, scaling, bond-counting convention, and continuum-limit construction, none of which is sourced sufficiently.

children.title: Boundary-Condition Dependence
children.top_down_role: Model sensitivity to domain-boundary conventions.

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary-Condition Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A discrete ramp receives different TV costs under Neumann and periodic boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(u_i=i\) on \(i=1,\ldots,n\), define one-dimensional forward-difference TV with a free terminal boundary by \[\operatorname{TV}_{N}(u)=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}|u_{i+1}-u_i|,\] and periodic TV by \[\operatorname{TV}_{P}(u)=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}|u_{i+1}-u_i|+|u_1-u_n|.\] Then \[\operatorname{TV}_{N}(u)=n-1,\qquad \operatorname{TV}_{P}(u)=2(n-1).\] Thus periodic closure adds a boundary jump absent under the free-boundary convention, changing the regularizer and potentially the optimizer even though all interior differences coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The same discrete ramp has twice the TV under periodic closure as under a free boundary because periodicity inserts an endpoint jump.
assumptions_latex: \(n\ge2\) and all forward differences have unit weight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{TV}_{P}(u)=2\operatorname{TV}_{N}(u)=2(n-1)\).

notation.meaning: Forward-difference TV with no wrap-around edge.
Forward-difference TV with a periodic wrap-around edge.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample kind fits the boundary-condition-dependence leaf and the arithmetic is correct under the stated conventions, but the record has no qualifying source and locator.

children.title: TV Nullspace Ambiguity
children.top_down_role: Ambiguity arising from invariant components and insufficient fidelity information.

children.title: Constant-Mode Nullspace
children.top_down_role: Global constant components left unpenalized by ordinary TV.

knowledge_statements.title: Constant-Mode Nullspace
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Kernel property of first-order discrete total variation on a connected grid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a connected undirected graph with an arbitrarily oriented incidence matrix \(D\in\mathbb{R}^{|E|\times |V|}\). For graph total variation \(\operatorname{TV}(x)=\|Dx\|_1\), one has \[\operatorname{null}(D)=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf 1_V\}.\] Consequently, for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^{|V|}\) and \(c\in\mathbb{R}\), \(\operatorname{TV}(x+c\mathbf 1_V)=\operatorname{TV}(x)\). Thus total variation alone cannot identify the global additive constant of a signal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a connected discretization graph, total variation vanishes exactly on constant signals and is unchanged by adding a global constant.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is an oriented vertex-edge incidence matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{null}(D)=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf 1_V\}\) and \(\operatorname{TV}(x+c\mathbf 1_V)=\operatorname{TV}(x)\).
review_flags: Exact graph-TV kernel statement requires a directly supporting source locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The graph-incidence kernel and TV invariance claims are mathematically standard and fit the property container, but no inspectable source locator is supplied.

children.title: Componentwise Nullspaces
children.top_down_role: Invariant components arising on disconnected or weakly coupled domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Componentwise Nullspaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nullspace structure when the TV discretization graph is disconnected.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have connected components \(V_1,\ldots,V_q\), and let \(D\) be an oriented incidence matrix. Then \[\operatorname{null}(D)=\left\{\sum_{j=1}^{q}c_j\mathbf 1_{V_j}:c_j\in\mathbb{R}\right\},\qquad \dim\operatorname{null}(D)=q.\] Hence \(\|Dx\|_1\) is invariant under independently adding a constant on each connected component. Any model using this seminorm must constrain or observe every component to remove all componentwise offsets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a graph with several connected components, TV cannot distinguish independent additive constants on those components.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is an oriented incidence matrix of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{null}(D)=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf 1_{V_1},\ldots,\mathbf 1_{V_q}\}\) and has dimension \(q\).
review_flags: Exact disconnected-graph nullspace statement requires a directly supporting source locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The componentwise kernel characterization is precise and fits the property container, but the exact disconnected-graph result has no cited source or locator.

children.title: Fidelity-Induced Ambiguity
children.top_down_role: Unresolved nullspace components under insufficient observation geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Fidelity-Induced Ambiguity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of data fidelity to resolve directions already invisible to total variation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(F(x)=\phi(Ax-b)+\lambda\|Dx\|_1\), where \(\lambda>0\), \(A\) and \(D\) are linear, and \(\phi\) depends only on its displayed argument. If a nonzero vector \(h\) satisfies \(Ah=0\) and \(Dh=0\), then \[F(x+th)=F(x)\quad\text{for every }x\text{ and }t\in\mathbb{R}.\] Therefore no fidelity term depending only on \(Ax\) can resolve a TV-null direction that also lies in \(\operatorname{null}(A)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A direction invisible to both the measurements and TV leaves the full objective unchanged, producing unavoidable ambiguity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x+th)=F(x)\) for all \(x\) and \(t\in\mathbb{R}\).
review_flags: The common-nullspace failure criterion lacks a supplied exact source locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The common-nullspace invariance statement fits this failure-boundary leaf and is mathematically plausible, but no supporting source locator is provided.

children.title: Solution Nonuniqueness
children.top_down_role: Multiplicity of admissible TV solutions caused by structural ambiguity.

knowledge_statements.title: Solution Nonuniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient common-nullspace condition for nonuniqueness of TV-regularized minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=\phi(Ax-b)+\lambda\|Dx\|_1\) on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), with \(\lambda>0\), and suppose \(x^\star\) minimizes \(F\). If \[\operatorname{null}(A)\cap\operatorname{null}(D)\ne\{0\},\] then every nonzero \(h\) in this intersection generates the affine family \(x^\star+th\), \(t\in\mathbb{R}\), of minimizers. Thus uniqueness requires at least \(\operatorname{null}(A)\cap\operatorname{null}(D)=\{0\}\), although this condition alone need not ensure uniqueness when other flat directions remain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero direction annihilated by both fidelity and TV generates an affine family of solutions; eliminating it is necessary, but not always sufficient, for uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star+th\in\operatorname{argmin}F\) for every \(t\in\mathbb{R}\) and every \(h\in\operatorname{null}(A)\cap\operatorname{null}(D)\).
review_flags: The sufficient nonuniqueness condition lacks a supplied exact source locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition correctly describes affine nonuniqueness from a common nullspace, but it lacks a source locator and does not explicitly specify the codomains of A and D or the domain of phi.

children.title: Line-Spectral Atomic Models
children.top_down_role: Continuous-frequency atoms for spectrally sparse signals.

knowledge_statements.title: Line-Spectral Atomic Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite complex exponentials sampled at consecutive integer times.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an integer \(n\ge1\), define \(a(f)=(1,e^{i2\pi f},\ldots,e^{i2\pi f(n-1)})^{\mathsf T}\) for \(f\in[0,1)\), and let \(\mathcal A=\{e^{i\varphi}a(f):f\in[0,1),\ \varphi\in[0,2\pi)\}\). A line-spectral signal is any \(x\in\mathbb C^n\) admitting \[x=\sum_{k=1}^{s}c_k a(f_k)\] with finitely many frequencies \(f_k\) and coefficients \(c_k\in\mathbb C\). Its atomic norm is \(\|x\|_{\mathcal A}=\inf\{\sum_k|c_k|:x=\sum_kc_ka(f_k)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A line-spectral signal is a finite sum of continuously indexed complex sinusoids; the atomic norm minimizes the total coefficient magnitude over such decompositions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is line-spectral exactly when it has a finite decomposition \(x=\sum_{k=1}^{s}c_k a(f_k)\).
review_flags: No line-spectral atomic-norm source locator was supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and atomic-norm normalization are coherent for phase-symmetric line-spectral atoms, but no authoritative source locator supports them.

children.title: Sparse-Measure Models
children.top_down_role: Finite-support measures on continuous domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse-Measure Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-support Radon measures on a continuous parameter domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Theta\) be a locally compact Hausdorff space. A finite signed or complex Radon measure \(\mu\) on \(\Theta\) is sparse when \[\mu=\sum_{k=1}^{s}c_k\delta_{\theta_k}\] for some finite \(s\), distinct points \(\theta_k\in\Theta\), and nonzero weights \(c_k\). Its sparsity is \(|\operatorname{supp}\mu|=s\), and its total-variation norm is \(\|\mu\|_{\mathrm{TV}}=\sum_{k=1}^{s}|c_k|\). Measurements generated by continuous functions \(g_j\) satisfy \(y_j=\int_\Theta g_j(\theta)\,d\mu(\theta)=\sum_kc_kg_j(\theta_k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sparse measure is a finite weighted sum of point masses on a continuous domain, with total variation equal to the sum of absolute weights.
assumptions_latex: \(\mu\) is a finite signed or complex Radon measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mu\) is sparse when \(\mu=\sum_{k=1}^{s}c_k\delta_{\theta_k}\) for finitely many support points.

notation.meaning: Dirac measure at the point theta

review_flags: No sparse-measure or measure-total-variation source locator was supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-support measure definition fits the leaf, but no source is cited. On a noncompact locally compact space, continuity of g_j alone does not guarantee integrability against every finite measure, so the measurement clause also requires an integrability or boundedness qualification.

children.title: Continuous-Dictionary Models
children.top_down_role: Parametric atoms beyond Fourier and point-mass families.

knowledge_statements.title: Continuous-Dictionary Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Atomic sparsity for a general continuously parameterized dictionary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Theta\) be a topological parameter space and let \(a:\Theta\to\mathbb F^n\), with \(\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}\), be a continuous atom map. The associated continuous-dictionary model of order at most \(s\) is \[\mathcal M_s=\left\{\sum_{k=1}^{r}c_k a(\theta_k):0\le r\le s,\ c_k\in\mathbb F,\ \theta_k\in\Theta\right\}.\] For the balanced atomic set generated by \(a(\Theta)\), the atomic gauge is the infimum of \(\sum_k|c_k|\) over all finite representations of \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous-dictionary model consists of signals represented by few atoms indexed by a continuous parameter, with an atomic gauge measuring minimum coefficient mass.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal M_s\) is the set of combinations of at most \(s\) continuously parameterized atoms.

notation.meaning: Atom indexed by a continuous parameter
Model using at most s atoms

review_flags: No general continuous-dictionary atomic-model source locator was supplied.

children.title: Moment-Matrix Lifts
children.top_down_role: Structured semidefinite representations based on moment matrices.

knowledge_statements.title: Moment-Matrix Lifts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-measure moments represented by positive semidefinite moment matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subset\mathbb R^d\), let \(v_r(t)\) collect all monomials of degree at most \(r\), and let \(y=(y_\alpha)_{|\alpha|\le2r}\) satisfy \(y_\alpha=\int_K t^\alpha\,d\mu(t)\) for a finite positive measure \(\mu\). The moment matrix defined by \([M_r(y)]_{\alpha,\beta}=y_{\alpha+\beta}\) obeys \[M_r(y)=\int_K v_r(t)v_r(t)^{\mathsf T}\,d\mu(t)\succeq0.\] Thus linear constraints on moments can be lifted to affine constraints on a structured positive semidefinite matrix; positivity alone need not ensure a representing measure on an arbitrary \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Moments of a positive measure form a structured positive semidefinite matrix, enabling a semidefinite lift, though PSD alone may not guarantee representability.
assumptions_latex: \(\mu\) is a finite positive measure supported on \(K\subset\mathbb R^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_r(y)=\int_Kv_r(t)v_r(t)^{\mathsf T}\,d\mu(t)\succeq0\).

notation.meaning: Moment indexed by the multi-index alpha
Vector of monomials through degree r

children.title: Toeplitz Semidefinite Lifts
children.top_down_role: Toeplitz-structured representations for compatible spectral atom families.

knowledge_statements.title: Toeplitz Semidefinite Lifts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semidefinite representation of the one-dimensional line-spectral atomic norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in\mathbb C^n\), let \(T(u)\) be the Hermitian Toeplitz matrix whose first column is \(u\). With atoms \(a(f)=(1,e^{i2\pi f},\ldots,e^{i2\pi f(n-1)})^{\mathsf T}\), the phase-symmetric atomic norm satisfies \[\|x\|_{\mathcal A}=\inf_{u,t}\left\{\frac{1}{2n}\operatorname{tr}T(u)+\frac{t}{2}:\begin{pmatrix}T(u)&x\\x^*&t\end{pmatrix}\succeq0\right\}.\] This lift applies to consecutive one-dimensional Fourier samples and uses the positive-semidefinite Vandermonde decomposition of Hermitian Toeplitz matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For consecutive one-dimensional Fourier samples, the line-spectral atomic norm equals an SDP involving a Hermitian Toeplitz matrix and one scalar.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A\) is the phase-symmetric line-spectral atomic set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|x\|_{\mathcal A}\) equals the displayed Toeplitz semidefinite program.

notation.meaning: Hermitian Toeplitz matrix with first column u

review_flags: The exact normalization and Vandermonde-based SDP identity require a line-spectral atomic-norm source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Toeplitz SDP representation has the appropriate mathematical role and regime, but its exact normalization and Vandermonde-based equality require a directly supporting source locator.

children.title: Trigonometric Atom Regimes
children.top_down_role: Continuous spectral settings supporting structured lift representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Trigonometric Atom Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sampling regime in which the standard Toeplitz lift is exact.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the observed atom be \(a_\Omega(f)=(e^{i2\pi fm})_{m\in\Omega}\) for a finite index set \(\Omega\subset\mathbb Z\). The standard single-level \(n\times n\) Toeplitz lift applies directly when, up to translation, \(\Omega=\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}\). In that regime, atom outer products depend only on index differences and satisfy \([a(f)a(f)^*]_{jk}=e^{i2\pi f(j-k)}\), producing Hermitian Toeplitz moment matrices. Nonconsecutive or multidimensional index sets generally require completion, multilevel Toeplitz structure, or another representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The standard Toeplitz lift matches consecutive one-dimensional trigonometric samples; irregular or multidimensional sampling generally needs additional structure.
assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\subset\mathbb Z\) is a finite sampling index set.
Atoms are complex exponentials indexed by \(f\in[0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\Omega\) is a translated consecutive interval, atom moment matrices are Hermitian Toeplitz and admit the standard lift.

notation.meaning: Trigonometric atom restricted to the sampling set

review_flags: The boundary between direct, completion-based, and multilevel Toeplitz regimes needs a specialized source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The consecutive-sample Toeplitz observation is sound, but the broader boundary involving irregular and multidimensional sampling is source-sensitive and presently unsupported.

children.title: Lift Representability Limits
children.top_down_role: Atom families lacking finite structured semidefinite lifts of the selected type.

knowledge_statements.title: Lift Representability Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of exact finite-dimensional semidefinite representability for continuous atomic gauges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a compact atomic set and let \(B_{\mathcal A}=\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A)\). An exact finite semidefinite lift exists only if there are an integer \(m\), an affine subspace \(L\subset\mathbb S^m\), and a linear map \(\pi:\mathbb S^m\to\mathbb R^n\) such that \[B_{\mathcal A}=\pi\bigl(L\cap\mathbb S_+^m\bigr).\] Compactness and convexity alone do not imply such representability. Therefore Toeplitz or moment lifts cannot be assumed exact for arbitrary continuous dictionaries without a dictionary-specific representation theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous atomic ball has an exact finite SDP lift only when it is a spectrahedral shadow; arbitrary compact dictionaries need not satisfy this.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact finite SDP lifting requires \(B_{\mathcal A}=\pi(L\cap\mathbb S_+^m)\) for some finite \(m\), affine \(L\), and linear \(\pi\).

notation.meaning: Cone of m-by-m positive semidefinite matrices

children.title: Measure Linear-Program Representations

knowledge_statements.title: Measure Linear-Program Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Atomic gauges represented as linear optimization over positive measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Theta\) be compact, let \(a:\Theta\to\mathbb R^n\) be continuous, and let \(\mathcal A=a(\Theta)\). For every \(x\) in the conic hull of \(\mathcal A\), its positive atomic gauge has the measure linear-program representation \[\gamma_{\mathcal A}^+(x)=\inf_{\mu\in\mathcal M_+(\Theta)}\left\{\mu(\Theta):x=\int_\Theta a(\theta)\,d\mu(\theta)\right\}.\] For signed coefficients, replacing positive measures by finite signed measures and \(\mu(\Theta)\) by \(\|\mu\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\) gives the balanced atomic gauge, subject to the same synthesis constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An atomic gauge equals minimum measure mass under a linear synthesis constraint; signed measures and total variation represent balanced atomic models.
assumptions_latex: \(\Theta\) is compact and \(a:\Theta\to\mathbb R^n\) is continuous.
\(x\) lies in the conic hull of \(a(\Theta)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_{\mathcal A}^+(x)=\inf\{\mu(\Theta):\mu\ge0,\ x=\int_\Theta a(\theta)\,d\mu(\theta)\}\).

notation.meaning: Finite positive Radon measures on the parameter space
Total-variation norm of a signed measure

children.title: Grid-Discretized Atomic Models
children.top_down_role: Finite dictionaries approximating continuous atom sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Grid-Discretized Atomic Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dictionary restriction of a continuous atomic gauge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal H\) be a finite-dimensional real or complex Hilbert space, let \(a:\Theta\to\mathcal H\) be an atom map, and choose a finite grid \(G\subset\Theta\). The grid dictionary is \(\mathcal A_G=\{a(t):t\in G\}\), and its atomic gauge is
\[\gamma_G(x)=\inf\left\{\sum_{t\in G}|c_t|:x=\sum_{t\in G}c_ta(t)\right\},\]
with value \(+\infty\) when no such coefficients exist. Thus the model domain is \(\operatorname{span}(\mathcal A_G)\), and optimization over the continuous atom family is replaced by finite-dimensional coefficient optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite parameter grid produces a finite atom dictionary whose atomic gauge is the minimum coefficient one-norm among all grid-supported representations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}\gamma_G=\operatorname{span}(\mathcal A_G)\).

children.title: Continuous-Atom Resolution Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Identifiability and approximation limits specific to continuous atoms.

children.title: Separation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Geometric regimes controlling distinguishability of nearby atoms.

assumptions_latex: \(s\geq2\) and \((t_i)_{i=1}^s\in\Theta^s\) is an indexed active family.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Delta(t_1,\ldots,t_s)\geq\rho\) characterizes the separated regime.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: minimum pairwise distance is the conventional separation predicate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-separation condition for continuous atoms under a parameter metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((\Theta,d)\) be a metric parameter space, let \(s\geq2\), and let \((t_i)_{i=1}^s\in\Theta^s\) be an indexed family of active parameters. Define
\[\Delta(t_1,\ldots,t_s)=\min_{1\leq i<j\leq s}d(t_i,t_j).\]
For a prescribed resolution scale \(\rho>0\), the separated regime is the predicate \(\Delta(t_1,\ldots,t_s)\geq\rho\), the near-collision regime is \(0<\Delta(t_1,\ldots,t_s)<\rho\), and the collision regime is \(\Delta(t_1,\ldots,t_s)=0\). Any recovery guarantee using this terminology must specify both \(d\) and \(\rho\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An indexed active family is separated when every pair of parameters is at least a prescribed resolution distance apart; positive smaller distances define near-collision, while zero distance defines collision.
knowledge_statements.title: Separation Regimes

children.title: Collision-Induced Identifiability Failure
children.top_down_role: Loss of distinguishability among closely spaced or equivalent atoms.

children.title: Atom-Collision Regimes
children.top_down_role: Parameter configurations where distinct atoms become difficult to separate.

knowledge_statements.title: Atom-Collision Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact and limiting collisions in a continuous atom map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(a:\Theta\to\mathcal H\) be continuous and consider \(x_n=c_{1,n}a(t_{1,n})+c_{2,n}a(t_{2,n})\), where \(d(t_{1,n},t_{2,n})\to0\), \(t_{1,n},t_{2,n}\to t_0\), and \(c_{1,n}\to c_1\), \(c_{2,n}\to c_2\). Then
\[x_n\to(c_1+c_2)a(t_0).\]
At exact collision, the two coefficients are identifiable only through their sum: every pair \((c'_1,c'_2)\) satisfying \(c'_1+c'_2=c_1+c_2\) yields the same signal. Hence labeled two-atom parameterization fails to be injective on the collision boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: As two continuous atoms collide, their contribution converges to one atom with the summed coefficient, so the individual colliding coefficients cannot be identified.
assumptions_latex: The two parameter sequences converge to \(t_0\).
The coefficient sequences have finite limits.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((c_1,c_2)\mapsto(c_1+c_2)a(t_0)\) is noninjective.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: continuity and coefficient merging give the stated collision limit
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The continuity limit and exact-collision noninjectivity are mathematically coherent, and failure_boundary fits the terminal container. No inspectable source is supplied.

children.title: Parameter Nonidentifiability
children.top_down_role: Ambiguity in continuous atom parameters.

assumptions_latex: Representations are compared modulo permutation, deletion of zero terms, and merging of repeated parameters by summing their coefficients.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The parameterization is nonidentifiable on \(D\) exactly when the induced map on reduced representation classes is noninjective.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: identifiability is injectivity modulo intrinsic representation symmetries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Injectivity criterion for a finite continuous-atom parameterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(a:\Theta\to\mathcal H\), let \(\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}\), and fix \(s\geq1\). Define the synthesis map
\[F_s((c_i,t_i)_{i=1}^s)=\sum_{i=1}^s c_i a(t_i)\]
on \((\mathbb F\times\Theta)^s\). Let \(D\subseteq(\mathbb F\times\Theta)^s\). Parameters are identifiable from the noiseless signal on \(D\) if \(F_s(c,t)=F_s(c',t')\) for two elements of \(D\) implies equality of their coefficient-parameter multisets after permutation, deletion of zero-coefficient terms, and merging of repeated parameters by summing their coefficients. Parameter nonidentifiability occurs precisely when this implication fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous-atom parameterization is nonidentifiable when two inequivalent admissible coefficient-parameter representations synthesize exactly the same noiseless signal.
knowledge_statements.title: Parameter Nonidentifiability

children.title: Equivalent Atom Representations
children.top_down_role: Distinct parameter descriptions producing indistinguishable atomic contributions.

knowledge_statements.title: Equivalent Atom Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence classes induced by the atomic synthesis map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let a finite atomic representation be a finitely supported coefficient function \(c:\Theta\to\mathbb F\), where \(\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}\), with synthesis \(S(c)=\sum_{t\in\Theta}c(t)a(t)\). Two representations \(c\) and \(c'\) are signal-equivalent when
\[c\sim_S c'\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad S(c)=S(c').\]
They are distinct equivalent representations when additionally \(c\ne c'\). The atom model has a unique representation on a class \(C\) exactly when every equivalence class of \(\sim_S\) intersects \(C\) in at most one element.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two finite atomic representations are equivalent when their synthesized signals coincide; uniqueness means each synthesis-equivalence class contains at most one admissible representation.
assumptions_latex: Each coefficient function has finite support.
The atom map \(a:\Theta\to\mathcal H\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c\sim_Sc'\) if and only if \(S(c)=S(c')\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: equality under a synthesis map canonically induces representation equivalence
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The synthesis-induced equivalence relation is precise, and definition is the correct content kind for this leaf. No inspectable citation is supplied.

children.title: Resolution-Induced Ambiguity
children.top_down_role: Loss of distinguishability caused by finite observational resolution.

knowledge_statements.title: Resolution-Induced Ambiguity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Indistinguishability under bounded deterministic observation error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M:\mathcal H\to\mathcal Y\) be linear, and suppose observations obey \(y=Mx+e\) with \(\|e\|_{\mathcal Y}\leq\varepsilon\). Two model signals \(x_1,x_2\) are resolution-ambiguous at noise radius \(\varepsilon\) whenever
\[\|M(x_1-x_2)\|_{\mathcal Y}\leq2\varepsilon.\]
Indeed, their closed observation balls of radius \(\varepsilon\) intersect. Consequently, no estimator can uniquely distinguish \(x_1\) from \(x_2\) for every admissible error whenever this inequality holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two signals are ambiguous at noise level ε when their noiseless observations are at most 2ε apart, because one observation can then be consistent with both.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|M(x_1-x_2)\|_{\mathcal Y}\leq2\varepsilon\) precludes uniform unique discrimination.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: intersection of norm balls is characterized by center distance at most twice their radius
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: For norm-bounded deterministic errors, the stated two-radius ambiguity condition and conclusion are correct. The failure_boundary kind matches the leaf, but the record lacks an inspectable source.

children.title: Basis Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Modeling error caused by an atom basis that does not contain the true structure.

assumptions_latex: \(b_1,\ldots,b_m\) belong to a normed vector space over \(\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a(t)\notin V_B\) if and only if \(r_B(t)>0\).

notation.meaning: assumed synthesis dictionary and its synthesis operator

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: distance to a closed subspace is positive exactly outside that subspace
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of an assumed finite dictionary span to contain an off-model atom.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(b_1,\ldots,b_m\) belong to a normed vector space over \(\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}\), define \(Bz=\sum_{j=1}^m z_jb_j\), and let \(V_B=\operatorname{span}\{b_1,\ldots,b_m\}\). For a continuous-family atom \(a(t)\), basis mismatch at \(t\) means
\[a(t)\notin V_B.\]
If \(V_B\) is closed, this is equivalent to positivity of the best representation residual
\[r_B(t)=\inf_{z\in\mathbb F^m}\|a(t)-Bz\|.\]
A signal containing this atom with a nonzero coefficient lies outside the assumed model unless its residual in the quotient by \(V_B\) is canceled by other components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Basis mismatch occurs when a true continuous-family atom lies outside the span of the assumed finite dictionary, giving a positive best-representation residual when that span is closed, absent cancellation by other components.
knowledge_statements.title: Basis Mismatch

children.title: Grid Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Parameter error caused by restriction to a fixed sampling grid.

knowledge_statements.title: Grid Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameter-level mismatch between true atoms and a discretization grid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((\Theta,d)\) be a metric parameter space and let \(G\subset\Theta\) be a finite grid. For a true active set \(T\subset\Theta\), define its directed grid mismatch by
\[\delta(T,G)=\sup_{t\in T}\inf_{g\in G}d(t,g).\]
The model is on-grid exactly when \(T\subseteq G\), equivalently \(\delta(T,G)=0\) when \(G\) is finite. It is off-grid when \(\delta(T,G)>0\). This parameter mismatch is distinct from the signal-space error caused by replacing \(a(t)\) with a nearby grid atom.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Grid mismatch is the largest distance from a true active parameter to its nearest grid point; it vanishes exactly for an on-grid support.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta(T,G)=0\) if and only if \(T\subseteq G\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: directed distance to a finite grid precisely measures off-grid support mismatch
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The directed distance definition is mathematically correct for a finite nonempty grid, and definition fits the exact leaf. No inspectable source is supplied.

children.title: Off-Grid Approximation Error
children.top_down_role: Distortion incurred when continuous atoms are represented by nearby grid points.

knowledge_statements.title: Off-Grid Approximation Error
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lipschitz signal-space bound for nearest-grid atom replacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((\Theta,d)\) be metric, let \(a:\Theta\to\mathcal H\) satisfy \(\|a(t)-a(u)\|\leq Ld(t,u)\), and let \(x=\sum_{i=1}^s c_i a(t_i)\). Choose nearest grid points \(g_i\in G\) and set \(x_G=\sum_{i=1}^s c_i a(g_i)\). Then
\[\|x-x_G\|\leq L\sum_{i=1}^s|c_i|d(t_i,g_i)\leq L\delta(T,G)\sum_{i=1}^s|c_i|.\]
Thus the deterministic approximation error decreases at most linearly with the grid mismatch under Lipschitz atom regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a Lipschitz atom map, replacing each true atom by its nearest grid atom incurs error bounded by the grid mismatch times the coefficient one-norm.
assumptions_latex: Each active parameter has a selected nearest grid point.
The signal has a finite atomic expansion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|x-x_G\|\leq L\delta(T,G)\sum_i|c_i|\).

notation.meaning: Lipschitz constant of the atom map

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the bound follows directly from Lipschitz continuity and the triangle inequality
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Lipschitz approximation bound is precise and its property content kind fits the error leaf. It lacks an inspectable source citation.

children.title: Discretization Refinement Regimes
children.top_down_role: Changes in mismatch behavior as the parameter grid is refined.

assumptions_latex: \((\Theta,d)\) is a metric space and \(K\subseteq\Theta\) is compact.
Each \(G_k\subseteq K\) is a finite nonempty grid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{t\in K}\inf_{g\in G_k}\|a(t)-a(g)\|\to0\).

notation.meaning: k-th finite grid contained in K

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: uniform continuity transfers vanishing parameter fill distance to uniform atom approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence regimes for finite grids refining a compact parameter region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((\Theta,d)\) be a metric space, let \(K\subseteq\Theta\) be compact, and let \(G_k\subseteq K\) be finite nonempty grids. Define the fill distance
\[h_k=\sup_{t\in K}\inf_{g\in G_k}d(t,g).\]
If \(h_k\to0\), the grids form a refining regime on \(K\). For a uniformly continuous atom map \(a:K\to\mathcal H\),
\[\sup_{t\in K}\inf_{g\in G_k}\|a(t)-a(g)\|\to0.\]
If \(a\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, this supremum is at most \(Lh_k\). Refinement therefore controls atom approximation, although it alone does not ensure stable coefficient or parameter recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vanishing fill distance for grids contained in a compact parameter region yields uniform atom approximation for uniformly continuous atom maps, with a linear bound under Lipschitz regularity.
knowledge_statements.title: Discretization Refinement Regimes

children.title: Semidefinite Representability Limits
children.top_down_role: Continuous atom families without practical exact lifted representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Semidefinite Representability Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite semidefinite lifts require spectrahedral-shadow geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A convex set \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) has an exact finite semidefinite representation only if there exist symmetric matrices \(A_0,A_i,B_j\) of a common finite size such that
\[C=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists y\in\mathbb R^q,\ A_0+\sum_{i=1}^n x_iA_i+\sum_{j=1}^q y_jB_j\succeq0\right\}.\]
Thus \(C\) must be a spectrahedral shadow and, in particular, semialgebraic. Consequently, a continuous-atom unit ball known not to be semialgebraic, or known not to be a spectrahedral shadow, admits no exact finite semidefinite lift of this form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact finite SDP lift makes the atomic unit ball a spectrahedral shadow; failure of spectrahedral-shadow or semialgebraic geometry rules such a lift out.
assumptions_latex: Only finite-dimensional linear matrix inequality lifts are considered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) not a spectrahedral shadow implies that \(C\) has no exact finite semidefinite representation.

notation.meaning: convex set or atomic unit ball

children.title: Sum-of-Gauges Models
children.top_down_role: Additive regularization imposing multiple structural preferences.

knowledge_statements.title: Sum-of-Gauges Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive convex regularization for simultaneous structural preferences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional vector space, let \(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_m:V\to[0,+\infty]\) be closed convex gauges, and let \(\lambda_i>0\). The sum-of-gauges regularizer is
\[R(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\gamma_i(x).\]
It is a closed convex gauge when the sum is proper. Its unit sublevel set is
\[\{x:R(x)\leq1\}=\left\{x:\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\gamma_i(x)\leq1\right\},\]
which imposes every component penalty on the same variable rather than decomposing that variable into separately structured summands.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sum-of-gauges model adds positively weighted gauges of the same variable, producing a convex gauge that simultaneously penalizes several structural attributes.
assumptions_latex: Each \(\gamma_i\) is a closed convex gauge.
Each \(\lambda_i>0\), and the sum is proper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\gamma_i\) is a closed convex gauge.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: positive finite sums preserve convexity and positive homogeneity of proper closed gauges

auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite maximum of extended-valued gauges and its unit sublevel set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For gauges \(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_m\) on \(X\), define the maximum-gauge model by \[\gamma_{\max}(x):=\max_{1\le i\le m}\gamma_i(x).\] Then \(\gamma_{\max}\) is convex, nonnegative, positively homogeneous, and vanishes at the origin. Its unit sublevel set satisfies \[\{x\in X:\gamma_{\max}(x)\le 1\}=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\{x\in X:\gamma_i(x)\le 1\}.\] If every \(\gamma_i\) is finite, then \(\gamma_{\max}\) is finite; if at least one component is definite, then \(\gamma_{\max}(x)=0\) implies \(x=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite maximum of gauges is a gauge, and its unit ball is exactly the intersection of the component unit balls.

children.title: Intersection-Gauge Models
children.top_down_role: Composite models built from simultaneous membership in multiple gauge balls.

knowledge_statements.title: Intersection-Gauge Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constrained convex model imposing all structural gauges simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a real vector space, let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be convex, let \(\gamma_i:X\to[0,+\infty]\) be gauges, and let \(\tau_i>0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\). An intersection-gauge model has the form \[\inf_{x\in X} f(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad \gamma_i(x)\le \tau_i,\qquad i=1,\ldots,m.\] Defining \(\Gamma_{\tau}(x):=\max_{1\le i\le m}\gamma_i(x)/\tau_i\), its feasible region has the equivalent representation \[\bigcap_{i=1}^m\{x\in X:\gamma_i(x)\le\tau_i\}=\{x\in X:\Gamma_{\tau}(x)\le1\}.\] Thus feasibility requires simultaneous membership in every component sublevel set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simultaneous positive-radius gauge constraints are equivalent to one constraint on the maximum of the radius-normalized gauges.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real vector space and \(m<\infty\).
\(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is convex, each \(\gamma_i:X\to[0,+\infty]\) is a gauge, and \(\tau_i>0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_i(x)\le\tau_i\) for every \(i\) if and only if \(\max_{1\le i\le m}\gamma_i(x)/\tau_i\le1\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: simultaneous positive-radius gauge inequalities are algebraically equivalent to one normalized maximum-gauge inequality

children.title: Intersected Unit Balls
children.top_down_role: Convex geometry produced by intersecting constituent unit balls.

assumptions_latex: Each \(C_i\subset X\) is closed, convex, absorbing, and contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_{\cap_i C_i}(x)=\max_i\gamma_{C_i}(x)\) for every \(x\in X\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the Minkowski functional converts finite intersections into pointwise maxima
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minkowski functional identity for a finite intersection of absorbing convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_\cap:=\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\), and for any absorbing set \(C\) define its Minkowski functional by \[\gamma_C(x):=\inf\{t>0:x\in tC\}.\] The finite intersection \(C_\cap\) is closed, convex, absorbing, and contains \(0\). For every \(x\in X\), \[\gamma_{C_\cap}(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}\gamma_{C_i}(x).\] Consequently, when each \(C_i\) is the unit ball of a gauge \(\gamma_i\), the intersection is the unit ball of the maximum gauge \(\max_i\gamma_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Minkowski functional of finitely many intersected convex unit balls is the maximum of their individual Minkowski functionals.
knowledge_statements.title: Intersected Unit Balls

children.title: Constraint-Activity Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Activity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: KKT classification of active constraints in a finite convex intersection-gauge model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be finite-dimensional, let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex, and let each \(\gamma_i:X\to[0,+\infty)\) be a finite continuous gauge. Suppose there exists \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) such that \(\gamma_i(\bar x)<\tau_i\) for every \(i\). A feasible point \(x^\star\in\operatorname{dom}f\) minimizes \(f(x)\) subject to \(\gamma_i(x)\le\tau_i\) if and only if there are multipliers \(\lambda_i\ge0\) satisfying \[0\in\partial f(x^\star)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\partial\gamma_i(x^\star),\qquad \lambda_i\bigl(\gamma_i(x^\star)-\tau_i\bigr)=0\quad\text{for }i=1,\ldots,m.\] If \(\gamma_i(x^\star)<\tau_i\), then \(\lambda_i=0\). If \(\lambda_i>0\), then the corresponding constraint is active, although an active constraint may have zero multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a valid Slater condition, the convex KKT conditions characterize optimality: inactive constraints have zero multipliers, positive multipliers imply activity, and degenerate active constraints may also have zero multipliers.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex, and each \(\gamma_i:X\to[0,+\infty)\) is a finite continuous gauge.
There exists \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) with \(\gamma_i(\bar x)<\tau_i\) for every \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible \(x^\star\in\operatorname{dom}f\) is optimal if and only if stationarity, dual feasibility, and \(\lambda_i(\gamma_i(x^\star)-\tau_i)=0\) hold for suitable multipliers \(\lambda_i\ge0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The infimal-convolution gauge is \[\Gamma(x):=\inf_{z_1+\cdots+z_m=x}\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\gamma_i(z_i).\] Under the stated assumptions the infimum is attained, and \(\Gamma\) is a closed gauge. If \(B_i:=\{z\in X:\gamma_i(z)\le1\}\), then its unit ball is \[\{x:\Gamma(x)\le1\}=\operatorname{conv}\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^m\lambda_i^{-1}B_i\right).\] Thus the latent variables allocate each part of \(x\) to whichever component gauge represents it most economically.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Infimal convolution minimizes total gauge cost over latent decompositions and equals the gauge of the convex hull of scaled component balls.

children.title: Demixing Models
children.top_down_role: Separation of superposed components with distinct atomic structures.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex separation of linearly superposed components with distinct gauges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given data \(b\in Y\), positive weights \(\lambda_i\), and a convex data-fidelity function \(\ell:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), a demixing model is \[\inf_{x_i\in X_i}\;\ell\left(\sum_{i=1}^m M_i x_i-b\right)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\gamma_i(x_i).\] In the noiseless case, the fidelity term is replaced by the constraint \(\sum_iM_ix_i=b\). The variables \(x_i\) represent separately recoverable components, while their distinct gauges encode the structural differences used to separate the observed superposition.

children.title: Cross-Task Coupling

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Task Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-structured convex coupling through pairwise parameter differences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph on tasks \(V=\{1,\ldots,T\}\), let \(w_{st}\ge0\) be the weight of edge \(\{s,t\}\), and let \(\gamma:X\to[0,+\infty)\) be a norm. Define \[R_G(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_T):=\sum_{\{s,t\}\in E}w_{st}\gamma(\theta_s-\theta_t).\] The function \(R_G\) is convex and positively homogeneous in the stacked parameter. It vanishes exactly when \(\theta_s=\theta_t\) on every positive-weight edge. Consequently, the parameters are constant on each connected component of the positive-weight subgraph; if that subgraph is connected, then \(R_G(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_T)=0\) if and only if \(\theta_1=\cdots=\theta_T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph penalty couples tasks through normed pairwise parameter differences, and its nullspace consists of consensus parameters on each connected component of the positive-weight subgraph.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected task graph with \(V=\{1,\ldots,T\}\) and edge weights \(w_{st}\ge0\).
\(X\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space and \(\gamma:X\to[0,+\infty)\) is a norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_G(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_T)=\sum_{\{s,t\}\in E}w_{st}\gamma(\theta_s-\theta_t)\) vanishes exactly on componentwise consensus for the positive-weight subgraph.

notation.meaning: Norm used to measure task differences

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: graph total-variation penalties couple tasks through normed pairwise differences

children.title: Component Leakage Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Ambiguity between shared and task-specific latent components.

knowledge_statements.title: Component Leakage Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Descent-direction criterion for failure of unique recovery in a shared-specific gauge decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be finite-dimensional and suppose \(\theta_t^\star=u^\star+v_t^\star\) for \(t=1,\ldots,T\). For a convex gauge \(\gamma\), define \[D_\gamma(x):=\{h\in X:\gamma(x+\varepsilon h)\le\gamma(x)\text{ for some }\varepsilon>0\}.\] If there exists \(h\ne0\) such that \[h\in D_{\gamma_0}(u^\star)\cap\bigcap_{t=1}^T\bigl(-D_{\gamma_t}(v_t^\star)\bigr),\] then there is a sufficiently small \(\varepsilon>0\) for which \(u^\star+\varepsilon h\) and \(v_t^\star-\varepsilon h\) preserve every sum \(u^\star+v_t^\star\) and do not increase any component gauge. Therefore the starred decomposition is not the unique solution of a positive weighted-gauge minimization problem constrained only by those taskwise sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Leakage occurs when one nonzero direction can enter the shared component and leave every task-specific component without changing the task parameters or increasing any component gauge; then weighted-gauge minimization cannot uniquely recover the starred decomposition.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space and \(T<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A nonzero \(h\in D_{\gamma_0}(u^\star)\cap\bigcap_{t=1}^T[-D_{\gamma_t}(v_t^\star)]\) prevents unique recovery of the starred shared-specific decomposition by positive weighted-gauge minimization subject only to the taskwise sums.

notation.meaning: Gauge descent-direction set at a point

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: a common penalty-nonincreasing transfer direction preserves all taskwise sums and obstructs unique decomposition recovery

notation.meaning: Tangent space of component model i at its component point.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order identifiability boundary for an additive two-component model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space, let \(M_1,M_2\subset E\) be smooth component models near \(x_1\in M_1\) and \(x_2\in M_2\), and define \(F:M_1\times M_2\to E\) by \(F(u,v)=u+v\). If \(T_{M_1}(x_1)\cap T_{M_2}(x_2)\neq\{0\}\), then \[\ker DF(x_1,x_2)\neq\{0\}.\] Thus the component pair is not identifiable to first order from its sum at \((x_1,x_2)\).

children.title: Component-Scaling Imbalance
children.top_down_role: Structural distortion caused by incompatible gauge scaling.

knowledge_statements.title: Component-Scaling Imbalance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Allocation distortion produced by unequal regularization scales on a shared component ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a\neq0\), \(t>0\), and let gauges \(\gamma_1,\gamma_2\) satisfy \(0<\gamma_i(a)<\infty\). For decompositions \(ta=x_1+x_2\) restricted to \(x_1=\alpha a\), \(x_2=(t-\alpha)a\), and \(0\leq\alpha\leq t\), the weighted penalty equals \[\lambda_1\gamma_1(x_1)+\lambda_2\gamma_2(x_2)=\alpha\lambda_1\gamma_1(a)+(t-\alpha)\lambda_2\gamma_2(a).\] If \(\lambda_1\gamma_1(a)<\lambda_2\gamma_2(a)\), every minimizer assigns the whole ray to component one; the reverse inequality assigns it to component two. Equality makes every such allocation optimal and therefore nonidentifiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a direction admitted by both models, unequal effective gauge scales force the entire feature into the cheaper component; equal scales leave its allocation ambiguous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The allocation is an endpoint unless \(\lambda_1\gamma_1(a)=\lambda_2\gamma_2(a)\), in which case all \(\alpha\in[0,t]\) are optimal.

notation.meaning: Amount of the shared ray assigned to component one.

review_flags: The calculation is self-contained, but a source is needed for its use as a composite-model identifiability boundary.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ray-restricted calculation is mathematically precise, and failure_boundary fits the terminal container. No inspectable scholarly citation supports its interpretation as a composite-model identifiability boundary.

children.title: Polyhedral Gauge Representations

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Gauge Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact linear-program representation of a gauge generated by finitely many atoms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=[a_1\ \cdots\ a_N]\in\mathbb R^{d\times N}\), and let \(C=\operatorname{conv}(\{0,a_1,\ldots,a_N\})\). The extended gauge of \(C\) has the exact linear representation \[\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}c:Ac=x,\ c\in\mathbb R_+^N\}.\] Consequently its epigraph is the projection of the polyhedron \[\{(x,t,c):Ac=x,\ c\geq0,\ \mathbf1^{\mathsf T}c\leq t\}.\] Conversely, every closed polyhedral gauge has a polyhedral unit sublevel set and admits a finite linear description, possibly after introducing auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-atom gauge is the optimal value of a linear program, and its epigraph is a projected polyhedron.
assumptions_latex: The gauge is allowed to take value \(+\infty\) outside \(\operatorname{cone}(A)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}\gamma_C=\operatorname{proj}_{x,t}\{(x,t,c):Ac=x,\ c\geq0,\ \mathbf1^{\mathsf T}c\leq t\}\).

notation.meaning: Matrix whose columns are the atoms.

knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order-Cone Gauge Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact conic-quadratic lift for gauges assembled from Euclidean block norms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition \(x\in\mathbb R^d\) into blocks \(x_{G_1},\ldots,x_{G_m}\), and take weights \(w_j>0\). The grouped gauge \(\gamma(x)=\sum_{j=1}^m w_j\|x_{G_j}\|_2\) has the exact second-order-cone representation \[\gamma(x)=\min_{t\in\mathbb R_+^m}\left\{\sum_{j=1}^m w_jt_j:\ (t_j,x_{G_j})\in\mathcal Q_{1+|G_j|}\ \text{for every }j\right\},\] where \(\mathcal Q_k=\{(s,z)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{k-1}:\|z\|_2\leq s\}\). Thus its epigraph is a linear image of an affine slice of a product of Lorentz cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sum of weighted Euclidean block norms is represented exactly using one Lorentz-cone constraint per block.
assumptions_latex: \(G_1,\ldots,G_m\) form a partition of the coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}\gamma\) is second-order-cone representable.

notation.meaning: Epigraph variable bounding the j-th Euclidean block norm.

knowledge_statements.title: Semidefinite Gauge Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projected-spectrahedral representation, illustrated by the nuclear norm gauge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), the nuclear norm has the exact semidefinite representation \[\|X\|_*=\min_{U\in\mathbb S^m,\,V\in\mathbb S^n}\left\{\frac12\bigl(\operatorname{tr}U+\operatorname{tr}V\bigr):\begin{pmatrix}U&X\\X^{\mathsf T}&V\end{pmatrix}\succeq0\right\}.\] Hence its epigraph is the projection onto \((X,t)\) of the spectrahedron defined by the displayed linear matrix inequality together with \(\operatorname{tr}U+\operatorname{tr}V\leq2t\). More generally, a gauge is semidefinite representable when its epigraph is a linear projection of an affine slice of a positive-semidefinite cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The matrix nuclear norm is the optimal value of a semidefinite program, making its epigraph a projected spectrahedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}\|\cdot\|_*\) is semidefinite representable.

knowledge_statements.title: Measure-Space Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-measure representation of a gauge generated by a compact atom family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A\subset\mathbb R^d\) be compact, and put \(C=\operatorname{conv}(\{0\}\cup\mathcal A)\). For the cone \(\mathcal M_+(\mathcal A)\) of finite nonnegative Radon measures, define \(K\mu=\int_{\mathcal A}a\,d\mu(a)\). Then the extended atomic gauge satisfies \[\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{\mu(\mathcal A):\mu\in\mathcal M_+(\mathcal A),\ K\mu=x\}.\] The infimum is \(+\infty\) when \(x\notin\operatorname{cone}(\mathcal A)\). Thus a continuous or infinite atom family yields an exact linear optimization problem over a cone of measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The gauge of a compact atom family equals the least total mass of a nonnegative measure whose atom barycenter is the target point.
assumptions_latex: Measures are finite, nonnegative, and Radon.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{\mu(\mathcal A):K\mu=x,\ \mu\geq0\}\).

notation.meaning: Cone of finite nonnegative Radon measures on the atom set.
Extended gauge of the convex atomic unit set.

children.title: Infinite-Dimensional Conic Forms
