knowledge_statements.title: Infinite-Dimensional Conic Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conic-program form of finite-dimensional observations synthesized from nonnegative measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A\) be compact, let \(K:\mathcal M(\mathcal A)\to\mathbb R^d\) be weak-star continuous and linear, and let \(b\in\mathbb R^p\). A measure-based low-complexity problem has the conic form \[\inf_{\mu\in\mathcal M_+(\mathcal A)}\left\{\langle c,K\mu\rangle+\tau\mu(\mathcal A):BK\mu=b\right\},\] with \(\tau\geq0\) and linear \(B:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^p\). Its decision cone is infinite-dimensional, while its objective and constraints depend only on finitely many moments \((K\mu,\mu(\mathcal A))\). This separates the infinite-dimensional representation from the finite-dimensional observation interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Measure optimization is a conic program over nonnegative measures whose objective and constraints access only finitely many moments.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A\) is compact and \(K\) is weak-star continuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The problem is a linear conic program over \(\mathcal M_+(\mathcal A)\) with a finite-dimensional moment interface.

notation.meaning: Linear observation map acting on the moments.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conic Caratheodory support bound for an attained atomic-gauge representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A\subset\mathbb R^d\) be compact, let \(C=\operatorname{conv}(\{0\}\cup\mathcal A)\), and define \(K\mu=\int_{\mathcal A}a\,d\mu(a)\). Suppose the measure formulation of the atomic gauge at \(x\in\mathbb R^d\) attains the finite value \(t=\gamma_C(x)\). Then there exists an optimal measure \(\widehat\mu\in\mathcal M_+(\mathcal A)\) such that \[K\widehat\mu=x,\qquad \widehat\mu(\mathcal A)=t,\qquad |\operatorname{supp}\widehat\mu|\leq d+1.\] This is an existence statement and does not assert uniqueness.

knowledge_statements.title: Representability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between finite linear lifts and genuinely nonpolyhedral atomic gauge balls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^d\) be a closed convex set containing the origin, and let \(\gamma_C\) be its gauge. If \(\operatorname{epi}\gamma_C\) is the projection of a polyhedron described by finitely many linear inequalities, then \(\operatorname{epi}\gamma_C\), and hence the unit sublevel set \(C=\{x:\gamma_C(x)\leq1\}\), is polyhedral. Therefore a nonpolyhedral atomic unit ball cannot possess an exact finite linear-program lift. In particular, for \(d\geq2\), the Euclidean unit ball generated by the unit sphere is not polyhedral, so its measure representation cannot be replaced exactly by finitely many atomic LP columns, although it has a second-order-cone representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact finite LP lift forces a polyhedral gauge ball; the Euclidean ball therefore needs a richer cone or an approximation.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is closed, convex, and contains the origin.
The proposed lift uses finitely many linear inequalities and auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}\gamma_C\text{ has a finite polyhedral lift}\Longrightarrow C\text{ is polyhedral}.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A_h\subseteq\mathcal A\subset\mathbb R^d\), and define \(C_h=\operatorname{conv}(\{0\}\cup\mathcal A_h)\) and \(C=\operatorname{conv}(\{0\}\cup\mathcal A)\). Then \(C_h\subseteq C\), and their extended gauges satisfy \[\gamma_{C_h}(x)\geq\gamma_C(x)\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb R^d.\] Thus restricting the atom family gives an inner approximation of the unit set and a possibly infinite overestimate of the original gauge. Enlarging the restricted family monotonically enlarges \(C_h\) and decreases \(\gamma_{C_h}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricting the atom set shrinks the unit ball and can only increase the corresponding gauge; adding atoms improves the approximation monotonically.

children.title: Outer Gauge Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Tractable outer approximations to gauge balls or epigraphs.

knowledge_statements.title: Outer Gauge Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimistic gauge bound obtained from a tractable outer approximation of the unit ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\subseteq R\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be closed convex sets containing the origin, where \(B\) is the exact gauge unit set and \(R\) is a tractable outer relaxation. Their extended gauges obey \[\gamma_R(x)\leq\gamma_B(x)\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb R^d.\] Consequently, replacing \(\gamma_B\) by \(\gamma_R\) in a minimization objective gives an optimistic lower surrogate for the penalty, while imposing \(x\in R\) instead of \(x\in B\) relaxes feasibility. If additionally \(R\subseteq\rho B\) for \(\rho\geq1\), then \(\rho^{-1}\gamma_B(x)\leq\gamma_R(x)\leq\gamma_B(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enlarging a gauge ball lowers its gauge. A multiplicative set containment provides matching multiplicative bounds on the relaxed penalty.
assumptions_latex: \(B\subseteq R\) are closed, convex, and contain the origin.
For the quantitative bound, \(R\subseteq\rho B\) with \(\rho\geq1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\subseteq R\subseteq\rho B\Longrightarrow\rho^{-1}\gamma_B\leq\gamma_R\leq\gamma_B.\)

children.title: Discretized Continuous-Atom Approximations

knowledge_statements.title: Discretized Continuous-Atom Approximations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite inner approximation of a compact continuously parameterized atomic family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Theta\) be a compact metric space, let \(a:\Theta\to\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfy \(\|a(\theta)-a(\theta')\|_2\le Ld(\theta,\theta')\), and define \(K=\operatorname{conv}(a(\Theta))\). For a finite \(\delta\)-net \(\Theta_\delta\subset\Theta\), the discretized atomic model is \(K_\delta=\operatorname{conv}\{a(\theta):\theta\in\Theta_\delta\}\). It is an inner approximation, \(K_\delta\subseteq K\), and its Euclidean Hausdorff error satisfies \(d_H(K_\delta,K)\le L\delta\). Consequently, any sequence of grids with \(\delta_k\to0\) yields \(d_H(K_{\delta_k},K)\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite parameter grid produces an inner atomic hull whose Hausdorff error is at most the atom map's Lipschitz constant times the grid resolution.
assumptions_latex: \(\Theta\) is compact and \(\Theta_\delta\) is a finite \(\delta\)-net.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K_\delta\subseteq K\) and \(d_H(K_\delta,K)\le L\delta\).

children.title: Hierarchical Semidefinite Approximations

knowledge_statements.title: Hierarchical Semidefinite Approximations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Moment-based outer hierarchy for compact basic semialgebraic atom families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\{t\in\mathbb{R}^p:g_j(t)\ge0,\ j=1,\ldots,m\}\) be compact, let \(a:S\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be polynomial, and set \(K=\operatorname{conv}(a(S))\). At relaxation order \(d\), replace representing measures on \(S\) by truncated moment vectors whose moment and localizing matrices are positive semidefinite, obtaining a spectrahedral shadow \(K_d\). Under an Archimedean quadratic-module condition and consistent degree truncation, \(K\subseteq K_{d+1}\subseteq K_d\), and \(\bigcap_{d\ge d_0}K_d=K\). Thus increasing \(d\) gives successively tighter lifted semidefinite outer approximations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Truncated moment constraints give nested semidefinite outer approximations that converge to the convex hull of a compact polynomial atom family under an Archimedean condition.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is a compact basic semialgebraic set.
The quadratic module generated by \(g_1,\ldots,g_m\) is Archimedean.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\subseteq K_{d+1}\subseteq K_d\) and \(\bigcap_{d\ge d_0}K_d=K\).

notation.meaning: convex hull of the algebraic atom family

knowledge_statements.title: Proximal-Mapping Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle contract for a proper closed convex penalty on a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite-dimensional Hilbert space \(H\), a proper closed convex function \(\phi:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), a query \(z\in H\), and a parameter \(\lambda>0\), the proximal interface returns \[\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda\phi}(z)=\arg\min_{x\in H}\left\{\phi(x)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|x-z\|^2\right\}.\] The quadratic term makes the minimizer unique. An implementation must accept \((z,\lambda)\), return this minimizer to its declared numerical tolerance, and may exploit a gauge-, norm-, or penalty-specific routine without exposing an explicit lifted representation of \(\phi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interface returns the unique minimizer of a convex penalty plus a scaled squared distance to the query point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The oracle output is the unique point \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda\phi}(z)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Minimization Oracle Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle contract for optimization over a compact atomic hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and compact, and let \(K=\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A)\). On input \(g\in\mathbb{R}^n\), a linear-minimization oracle returns any \[s(g)\in\arg\min_{s\in K}\langle g,s\rangle.\] Because a linear functional attains its minimum over the compact hull at an atom, the interface may equivalently return \(a(g)\in\arg\min_{a\in\mathcal A}\langle g,a\rangle\). An approximate interface with additive tolerance \(\varepsilon\ge0\) may return \(\tilde s\in K\) satisfying \(\langle g,\tilde s\rangle\le\min_{s\in K}\langle g,s\rangle+\varepsilon\).

children.title: Primal-Ball Projection

knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Ball Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean projection onto the closed unit ball of a norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\|\cdot\|\) be a norm on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(B=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\|x\|\le1\}\), and take a query \(z\in\mathbb{R}^n\). The primal-ball projection interface returns the unique solution \[\Pi_B(z)=\arg\min_{x\in B}\frac12\|x-z\|_2^2.\] It returns \(z\) whenever \(\|z\|\le1\); otherwise its output lies on the boundary \(\{x:\|x\|=1\}\). A radius-\(\tau\) interface, with \(\tau>0\), is obtained by \(\Pi_{\tau B}(z)=\tau\Pi_B(z/\tau)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interface returns the unique Euclidean nearest point in a norm ball, with a scaling rule for arbitrary positive radii.
assumptions_latex: \(\tau>0\) when a nonunit radius is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pi_B(z)\) uniquely minimizes Euclidean squared distance over \(B\).

children.title: Dual-Ball Projection

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Ball Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean projection onto the unit ball of the dual norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a norm \(\|\cdot\|\) on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), define its dual norm by \(\|y\|_*=\sup_{\|x\|\le1}\langle y,x\rangle\) and its dual unit ball by \(B_*=\{y:\|y\|_*\le1\}\). Given \(z\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the interface returns \[\Pi_{B_*}(z)=\arg\min_{y\in B_*}\frac12\|y-z\|_2^2.\] The solution is unique and satisfies the Moreau identity \(\Pi_{B_*}(z)=z-\operatorname{prox}_{\|\cdot\|}(z)\), where the proximal parameter equals one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interface projects onto the dual-norm unit ball; equivalently, it subtracts the primal norm's unit-parameter proximal point from the query.
assumptions_latex: Projection and proximity use the Euclidean inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pi_{B_*}(z)=z-\operatorname{prox}_{\|\cdot\|}(z)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Polar-Set Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean projection onto the polar of a closed convex set containing the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, convex, and contain \(0\). Given \(z\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the polar-set projection interface returns \[\Pi_{C^\circ}(z)=\arg\min_{y\in C^\circ}\frac12\|y-z\|_2^2.\] The feasible set is nonempty, closed, and convex, so the output exists and is unique. If \(C\) is the unit ball of a norm, then \(C^\circ\) is its dual unit ball.

knowledge_statements.title: Flow-Based Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection onto a capacitated network-flow polytope through a convex flow problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a directed graph have node-arc incidence matrix \(D\in\mathbb{R}^{v\times e}\), balance vector \(b\in\mathbb{R}^v\), and finite bounds \(\ell,u\in\mathbb{R}^e\) with \(\ell\le u\). Assume the flow polytope \(F=\{f\in\mathbb{R}^e:Df=b,\ \ell\le f\le u\}\) is nonempty. For a query \(z\in\mathbb{R}^e\), the flow-based projection interface returns \[\Pi_F(z)=\arg\min_f\left\{\frac12\|f-z\|_2^2:Df=b,\ \ell\le f\le u\right\}.\] This is a separable strictly convex minimum-cost flow problem and has a unique optimal flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto a feasible capacitated-flow polytope is the unique solution of a separable quadratic minimum-cost flow problem.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic-Solver Interfaces

knowledge_statements.title: Memory Footprint
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dense storage required by variables and symmetric cone blocks in a lifted model.

\(\pi:Z\to E\) is a prescribed recovery map and \(\Phi:E\to\mathcal Y\) records the target feature.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The relaxation has structural fidelity on \(U\subseteq R\) exactly when \(\Phi(\pi(z))\in\Phi(S)\) for every \(z\in U\).
review_flags: REQUEST_SOURCES: no supplied locator defines a general structural-fidelity predicate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fidelity is relative to an explicit feature map, recovery map, and subset of relaxed points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subseteq R\) be the relaxed points whose recoveries are relevant, typically the optimizer set. The representation has structural fidelity for \((S,\Phi)\) on \(U\) if \[\Phi(\pi(z))\in\Phi(S)\quad\text{for every }z\in U.\] Exact target fidelity is the stronger requirement \(\pi(U)\subseteq S\). An objective value may therefore be tight while structural fidelity fails: equality of optimal values imposes no general requirement that every relaxed optimizer recover the rank, sparsity, integrality, or other feature encoded by \(\Phi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Structural fidelity means that recovered relaxed points retain a specified target feature; exact fidelity requires recovery into the original feasible set.
knowledge_statements.title: Structural Fidelity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed feature-map predicate is internally intelligible, but no source establishes it as the intended notion of structural fidelity for this taxonomy leaf.

children.title: Tightness–Fidelity Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Regimes where computational simplification changes structural discrimination.

assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq R_1\subseteq R_2\subseteq E\) are nonempty feasible sets.
The linear objective \(c\in E\) has finite attained minima on all three sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_{R_2}(c)\leq v_{R_1}(c)\leq v_S(c)\), while structural fidelity need not follow the same ordering without additional recovery assumptions.

notation.meaning: optimal linear-objective value over a set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the monotone value ordering and the absence of automatic fidelity monotonicity.

source_refs.locator: 4.3.1 Shor's semidefinite relaxation scheme p. 161

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(v_C(c)=\min_{x\in C}\langle c,x\rangle\). Set inclusion gives the monotone bound \[v_{R_2}(c)\leq v_{R_1}(c)\leq v_S(c).\] Thus replacing \(R_2\) by the tighter relaxation \(R_1\) cannot worsen the minimization lower bound. No analogous implication holds for a structural feature \(\Phi\) unless compatible recovery maps are specified: a tighter feasible set can still contain optimizers whose recoveries violate \(\Phi(S)\), and a looser formulation can admit a recovery rule that preserves the feature on its optimizer set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nested tighter relaxations improve objective bounds monotonically, but feature preservation is not monotone unless the recovery maps satisfy additional compatibility conditions.
knowledge_statements.title: Tightness–Fidelity Tradeoffs

source_witnesses.locator: 4.3.1 Shor's semidefinite relaxation scheme p. 161

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Set inclusion supports the value ordering, but the cited Shor-relaxation locator does not clearly support the broader assertion that structural fidelity has no corresponding monotonicity under potentially different recovery maps.

children.title: Fidelity-Loss Regimes
children.top_down_role: Model classes or approximation levels where essential structure is obscured.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The matrix with unit diagonal and all off-diagonal entries \(-1/2\) lies in \(R\setminus\operatorname{conv}(S)\), exhibiting structural fidelity loss.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A three-variable elliptope point demonstrates loss of sign-correlation structure.

source_refs.locator: 3.4.2 The geometry of a max-cut relaxation p. 58

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_\star\) have diagonal entries \(1\) and off-diagonal entries \(-1/2\). Its eigenvalues are \(0,3/2,3/2\), so \(X_\star\in R\). Every matrix in \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\) satisfies the valid inequality \(X_{12}+X_{13}+X_{23}\geq-1\), because each sign vector makes this sum equal to \(3\) or \(-1\). However, \(X_\star\) gives the sum \(-3/2\). Hence \(X_\star\notin\operatorname{conv}(S)\), and the relaxation admits correlations that no distribution over sign atoms can reproduce.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The three-dimensional elliptope contains a rank-two correlation matrix violating a valid inequality for convex combinations of sign correlation matrices.
knowledge_statements.title: Fidelity-Loss Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: 3.4.2 The geometry of a max-cut relaxation p. 58

children.title: Facial Conditioning Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Numerical sensitivity caused by low-dimensional faces, absent interiority, or poor scaling.

children.title: Facial Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Low-dimensional facial structure relevant to solver behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone and \(F=\{x\in K:Ax=b\}\neq\varnothing\).
The affine space \(\{x:Ax=b\}\) does not meet \(\operatorname{ri}(K)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The conic system is facially degenerate because its minimal containing face \(K_{\min}\) is a proper face of \(K\).

notation.meaning: feasible set of the conic system
minimal face of the cone containing the feasible set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses facial degeneracy in the sense of feasible-set containment in a proper cone face.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.1 Facial structure, nondegeneracy and strict complementarity p. 37
4.4 Symmetries, Dual Cones, and Facial Structure p. 167
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the minimal containing face by \[K_{\min}=\bigcap\{G:G\text{ is a face of }K\text{ and }F\subseteq G\}.\] The feasible conic system is facially degenerate when \(K_{\min}\neq K\). Equivalently, all feasible points lie in a proper face of the declared cone, so the formulation has no feasible point in \(\operatorname{ri}(K)\). Replacing \(K\) by \(K_{\min}\) preserves \(F\) and restores relative interior feasibility whenever \(F\cap\operatorname{ri}(K_{\min})\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible conic system is facially degenerate when all feasible points lie in a proper face of its declared cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Facial Degeneracy

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.1 Facial structure, nondegeneracy and strict complementarity p. 37
4.4 Symmetries, Dual Cones, and Facial Structure p. 167

children.title: Numerical Conditioning
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity associated with scaling, perturbations, or local geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Numerical Conditioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adopts a normwise distance-to-ill-posedness condition number for optimization data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(d\notin\Sigma\), define \[\kappa(d)=\frac{\|d\|}{\operatorname{dist}(d,\Sigma)},\qquad \operatorname{dist}(d,\Sigma)=\inf_{s\in\Sigma}\|d-s\|.\] Set \(\kappa(d)=+\infty\) when \(d\in\Sigma\). A large value means that a perturbation small relative to \(\|d\|\) can reach ill-posed data and thereby change feasibility, boundedness, or another outcome used to define \(\Sigma\). The numerical conditioning therefore depends on the chosen data encoding, norm, and ill-posedness set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Numerical conditioning can be measured by data size divided by distance to ill-posed instances; proximity to ill-posedness produces a large condition number.
assumptions_latex: Problem data are represented by a nonzero vector \(d\) in a normed finite-dimensional data space \(\mathcal D\).
\(\Sigma\subseteq\mathcal D\) is the set of ill-posed data separating distinct qualitative outcomes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The relative condition number is \(\kappa(d)=\|d\|/\operatorname{dist}(d,\Sigma)\), with \(\kappa(d)=+\infty\) on \(\Sigma\).

source_refs.locator: 4.1.4 Stability and sensitivity analysis p. 86

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1.4 Stability and sensitivity analysis p. 86

children.title: Degeneracy-Induced Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Conditioning deterioration attributable to degenerate facial structure.

assumptions_latex: Sensitivity is measured by Hausdorff distance between optimizer sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The degenerate optimizer set at \(t=0\) is not Hausdorff-continuous under arbitrarily small nonzero objective perturbations.

notation.meaning: optimizer set of the parameterized problem

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A scalar linear program isolates sensitivity caused by a nonunique degenerate optimum.

source_refs.locator: 3.5.2 Sensitivity Analysis p. 61

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The optimizer mapping is \[S(t)=\begin{cases}\{-1\},&t>0,\\[-1,1],&t=0,\\\{1\},&t<0.\end{cases}\] Hence \(d_H(S(t),S(0))=2\) for every \(t\neq0\), although the objective perturbation magnitude \(|t|\) tends to zero. The optimal value \(-|t|\) remains continuous, but the optimizer set does not. Thus nonuniqueness at the degenerate parameter can destroy set-valued solution stability even when values are stable and the feasible region is unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A degenerate linear program can have a continuous optimal value while arbitrarily small objective perturbations cause a fixed-size jump in its optimizer set.
knowledge_statements.title: Degeneracy-Induced Sensitivity

source_witnesses.locator: 3.5.2 Sensitivity Analysis p. 61

children.title: Interiority Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Settings where absent or weak interiority creates numerical difficulty.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone and \(F=\{x\in K:Ax=b\}\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Interiority fails exactly when \(F\cap\operatorname{ri}(K)=\varnothing\); then the feasible set is confined to the boundary of the declared cone.

notation.meaning: feasible set of the conic system
minimal face containing the feasible set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers feasible conic systems that fail the primal Slater condition.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.1 Facial structure, nondegeneracy and strict complementarity p. 37

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The primal Slater condition is \(F\cap\operatorname{ri}(K)
eq\varnothing\). Its failure regime is therefore \[F
eq\varnothing\quad	ext{and}\quad F\cap\operatorname{ri}(K)=\varnothing.\] In this regime every feasible point lies on the relative boundary of \(K\), and the minimal face \(K_{\min}\) containing \(F\) is proper. Standard full-cone interior-point assumptions are unavailable in the original formulation. If \(F\cap\operatorname{ri}(K_{\min})
eq\varnothing\), facial reduction to \(K_{\min}\) yields an equivalent feasible system with relative interiority.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interiority fails when a feasible conic system has no feasible point in the cone's relative interior, forcing all feasible points into a proper face.
knowledge_statements.title: Interiority Failure Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.1 Facial structure, nondegeneracy and strict complementarity p. 37

children.title: Geometry–Template Matching
children.top_down_role: Selection of a gauge whose atoms and faces align with the desired structure.

children.title: Atom-Target Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Compatibility between elementary atoms and the target model.

children.title: Atom Family Suitability
children.top_down_role: Suitability of candidate atom families for the modeled structure.

assumptions_latex: \(E\) is finite-dimensional, \(\mathcal A\subset E\) is compact, and \(0\in\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A)\).
\(T\subset E\) is the target model and \(\gamma_{\mathcal A}\) is the gauge of \(\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The atom family is suitable for \(T\) under the stated criterion exactly when every normalized target admits an atomic decomposition attaining gauge one.
review_flags: REQUEST_SOURCES: no supplied locator supports a canonical atom-family suitability criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines suitability as exact normalized target coverage by gauge-attaining atomic decompositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\gamma_{\mathcal A}(x)=\inf\{t>0:x\in t\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A)\}\). The atomic family is suitable for the normalized target set \(T_1=\{x\in T:\gamma_{\mathcal A}(x)=1\}\) if, for every \(x\in T_1\), there exist atoms \(a_1,\ldots,a_k\in\mathcal A\) and coefficients \(\theta_i\geq0\) such that \[x=\sum_{i=1}^k\theta_i a_i\quad\text{and}\quad\sum_{i=1}^k\theta_i=1.\] Suitability fails when some target direction lies outside the cone generated by \(\mathcal A\), or only admits decompositions whose coefficient sum exceeds its intended normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An atom family is suitable when every normalized target has an atomic decomposition attaining the atomic gauge; uncovered target directions certify mismatch.
knowledge_statements.title: Atom Family Suitability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The criterion is not a meaningful suitability test: membership in the normalized set defined by \(\gamma_{\mathcal A}(x)=1\) already yields a coefficient-sum-one convex decomposition under the stated compactness assumptions. Directions outside the generated cone have infinite gauge and are excluded from that normalized set, so the asserted failure mode is not tested. A sourced, nonvacuous criterion is required.

children.title: Target Structure Coverage
children.top_down_role: Extent to which the atomic representation captures relevant target patterns.

knowledge_statements.title: Target Structure Coverage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Atomic-gauge coverage of a target model in a finite-dimensional vector space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space, let \(\mathcal A\subset X\) be compact, and suppose \(0\in\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A)\). Define \(C_{\mathcal A}=\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A)\) and \(\gamma_{\mathcal A}(x)=\inf\{t\geq 0:x\in tC_{\mathcal A}\}\), with infimum \(+\infty\) when the set is empty. An atomic template covers a target class \(\mathcal T\subset X\) when \(\mathcal T\subset\operatorname{cone}(C_{\mathcal A})\), equivalently \(\gamma_{\mathcal A}(x)<\infty\) for every \(x\in\mathcal T\). Uniform unit-scale coverage additionally requires \(\sup_{x\in\mathcal T}\gamma_{\mathcal A}(x)\leq 1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An atomic template covers the target class when every target is a finite nonnegative scaling of a convex combination of its atoms.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A\subset X\) is compact and \(0\in\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal T\) is covered exactly when \(\gamma_{\mathcal A}\) is finite on \(\mathcal T\).

notation.meaning: gauge generated by the convex hull of the atoms

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The gauge-based coverage definition is mathematically plausible and the definition content kind fits the leaf, but no source is supplied. The plain statement also omits the separately asserted uniform unit-scale coverage condition. An authoritative atomic-gauge locator is required before candidate acceptance.

children.title: Atom–Target Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Structural correspondence between selected atoms and target geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Atom–Target Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility combines representability with a target-adapted exposed atomic face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\gamma_{\mathcal A}\) be the atomic gauge generated by \(C_{\mathcal A}=\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A)\), and let \(x\neq0\) be a target. The dictionary is compatible with \(x\) if \(r=\gamma_{\mathcal A}(x)<\infty\) and there exists \(z\in X^*\) such that \(\langle z,a\rangle\leq1\) for every \(a\in\mathcal A\), \(\langle z,x\rangle=r\), and \(x/r\in\operatorname{conv}(F_z)\), where \(F_z=\{a\in\mathcal A:\langle z,a\rangle=1\}\). Thus the target admits an atomic decomposition supported on one face exposed by a dual certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compatibility means the target is representable and has a decomposition using atoms selected by one supporting functional of the atomic hull.
assumptions_latex: \(\gamma_{\mathcal A}\) is generated by a compact atomic set containing zero in its convex hull.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Compatibility holds when a dual functional exposes atoms whose convex hull contains \(x/\gamma_{\mathcal A}(x)\).

notation.meaning: atomic face exposed by the functional z
atomic gauge value of the target

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition content kind fits the compatibility leaf, but the proposed definition is uncited and nonstandard. Under the stated compactness assumptions, a nonzero target with finite gauge already lies on a supported boundary point after normalization, so the exposed-face clause appears automatic rather than a distinct compatibility requirement. A source must establish the intended stronger local meaning or motivate additional hypotheses.

children.title: Misalignment Failure Modes
children.top_down_role: Losses arising when atomic structure poorly matches the target class.

knowledge_statements.title: Misalignment Failure Modes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp representational failure caused by an atomic span that misses the target.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L=\operatorname{span}(\mathcal A)\subsetneq X\), let \(x_\star\in X\setminus L\), and let \(\gamma_{\mathcal A}\) be the gauge of \(\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A)\). Then \(\gamma_{\mathcal A}(x_\star)=+\infty\). Moreover, every atomic model point \(x\in L\) has approximation error at least \(\operatorname{dist}(x_\star,L)>0\) in any fixed norm. Consequently, an estimator constrained to the atomic span cannot recover \(x_\star\), even from noiseless injective observations; a penalized formulation using the extended-valued gauge either excludes the target or incurs irreducible approximation bias.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the atoms span a proper subspace missing the target, exact representation and recovery are impossible, with error at least the target’s distance to that span.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_{\mathcal A}(x_\star)=+\infty\) and \(\inf_{x\in L}\|x-x_\star\|=\operatorname{dist}(x_\star,L)>0\).

notation.meaning: linear span of the atomic dictionary
distance from the target to the atomic span

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, and failure of representability outside the atomic span is correct. However, the positive-distance conclusion requires the span to be closed, as it is in a finite-dimensional ambient space, while this record does not introduce X as finite-dimensional or otherwise assume L is closed. No supporting source is supplied.

children.title: Symmetry-Invariance Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Consistency between model symmetries and gauge invariances.

children.title: Target Symmetry Structure
children.top_down_role: Transformations under which the target model retains its structural identity.

knowledge_statements.title: Target Symmetry Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Group symmetry of a target class under a linear action.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a group \(G\) act linearly on a finite-dimensional real vector space \(X\). The symmetry group of a target class \(\mathcal T\subset X\) is \[G_{\mathcal T}=\{g\in G:g\mathcal T=\mathcal T\}.\] The target class is \(G\)-symmetric when \(G_{\mathcal T}=G\), equivalently, for every \(x\in\mathcal T\) and \(g\in G\), both \(gx\in\mathcal T\) and \(g^{-1}x\in\mathcal T\). Each orbit \(Gx=\{gx:g\in G\}\) then consists entirely of targets that are structurally equivalent under the declared action.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A target class is symmetric under a group when applying any group transformation preserves membership in the class.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a group acting linearly on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal T\) is \(G\)-symmetric exactly when \(g\mathcal T=\mathcal T\) for every \(g\in G\).

notation.meaning: orbit of x under the group action

children.title: Gauge Invariance Structure
children.top_down_role: Invariances encoded by the selected gauge or regularizer.

knowledge_statements.title: Gauge Invariance Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between gauge invariance and invariance of its unit sublevel set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset X\) be a closed convex set containing \(0\), and let \(\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{t\geq0:x\in tC\}\). Suppose a group \(G\) acts on \(X\) by invertible linear maps. Then \(\gamma_C(gx)=\gamma_C(x)\) for every \(g\in G\) and \(x\in X\) if and only if \(gC=C\) for every \(g\in G\). For an atomic gauge with \(C=\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A)\), it is sufficient that \(g\mathcal A=\mathcal A\) for every \(g\in G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gauge is group-invariant exactly when its unit set is group-invariant; invariance of the atom set is sufficient for an atomic gauge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_C(gx)=\gamma_C(x)\) for all \(g,x\) if and only if \(gC=C\) for all \(g\).

children.title: Symmetry–Invariance Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Consistency between target symmetries and representation invariances.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetry–Invariance Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility requires the regularizer to preserve every declared target symmetry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G_{\mathcal T}=\{g:g\mathcal T=\mathcal T\}\) be the target symmetry group and let \(G_R=\{g:R(gx)=R(x)\text{ for every }x\in X\}\) for a convex regularizer \(R:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\). The pair \((\mathcal T,R)\) is symmetry–invariance compatible when \(G_{\mathcal T}\subseteq G_R\). Equivalently, every structurally equivalent pair \(x,gx\) with \(x\in\mathcal T\) and \(g\in G_{\mathcal T}\) receives the same regularization value. For \(R=\gamma_C\), this condition is equivalent to \(gC=C\) for all \(g\in G_{\mathcal T}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regularizer is symmetry-compatible when it assigns equal values to all targets related by any declared target symmetry.
assumptions_latex: \(G_{\mathcal T}\) acts linearly and invertibly on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Compatibility is the inclusion \(G_{\mathcal T}\subseteq G_R\).

source_witnesses.locator: 4.4 Symmetries, Dual Cones, and Facial Structure p. 167

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the leaf, but the asserted equivalence is false as written. Equality R(gx)=R(x) only for x in the target class is weaker than membership of g in G_R, since G_R was defined by equality for every x in X. The cited section does not inspectably support this bespoke compatibility definition, so an authoritative source and a decision between global invariance and target-restricted invariance are required.

children.title: Broken-Invariance Failure Modes
children.top_down_role: Modeling failures caused by missing, excessive, or inappropriate invariance.

knowledge_statements.title: Broken-Invariance Failure Modes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetry breaking introduces orbit-dependent regularization and potentially arbitrary representative selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g\in G_{\mathcal T}\) and suppose a convex regularizer \(R\) satisfies \(R(gx_\star)\neq R(x_\star)\) for some \(x_\star\in\mathcal T\). If a loss \(L\) is invariant on this orbit, so that \(L(gx_\star)=L(x_\star)\), then for every \(\lambda>0\) the objectives \(L(x)+\lambda R(x)\) at \(x_\star\) and \(gx_\star\) differ by \(\lambda(R(gx_\star)-R(x_\star))\). Hence the regularized problem distinguishes structurally equivalent targets solely through broken regularizer invariance and favors whichever representative has smaller \(R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the loss respects a target symmetry but the regularizer does not, regularization favors one equivalent representative solely because of the symmetry mismatch.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The objective gap equals \(\lambda(R(gx_\star)-R(x_\star))\), so selection within the orbit is regularizer-induced.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed objective-gap identity is correct and the failure-boundary kind fits the leaf. However, it establishes only a pairwise preference between the two orbit representatives; without optimization or minimizer hypotheses it does not establish that the regularized problem globally selects either representative. No source is supplied for the broader failure interpretation.

children.title: Geometry Coupling Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Choice between separable, grouped, spectral, and coupled regularizers.

children.title: Decomposable Geometry
children.top_down_role: Separable or block-structured geometry supporting componentwise organization.

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposable Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact additive separability of a regularizer across a model subspace and its complement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional inner-product space, let \(\mathcal M\subseteq\overline{\mathcal M}\subseteq X\) be subspaces, and let \(R:X\to[0,+\infty)\) be a norm. The norm is decomposable with respect to \((\mathcal M,\overline{\mathcal M}^{\perp})\) when \[R(u+v)=R(u)+R(v)\] for every \(u\in\mathcal M\) and \(v\in\overline{\mathcal M}^{\perp}\). When \(\mathcal M=\overline{\mathcal M}\), this is exact additivity between the model subspace and its orthogonal complement; it excludes cross-block cancellation in the regularizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A norm has decomposable geometry when it is exactly additive between model directions and the designated orthogonal complement.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal M\subseteq\overline{\mathcal M}\subseteq X\) are linear subspaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Decomposability means \(R(u+v)=R(u)+R(v)\) for all \(u\in\mathcal M\) and \(v\in\overline{\mathcal M}^{\perp}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition content kind fits the leaf, and the stated decomposability identity is the standard model-subspace definition. Nevertheless, the record supplies neither a citation nor an explicit standard-field rationale, so it does not satisfy the evidence requirement.

children.title: Coupled Geometry
children.top_down_role: Geometry involving dependencies across components, groups, modes, or spectra.

knowledge_statements.title: Coupled Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonadditive regularizer interaction across prescribed structural components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=U\oplus V\) and let \(R:X\to[0,+\infty)\) be a norm. Define the coupling defect \[\Delta_R(u,v)=R(u+v)-R(u)-R(v),\qquad u\in U,\ v\in V.\] The geometry is coupled across \((U,V)\) when \(\Delta_R\) is not identically zero. Because every norm is subadditive, \(\Delta_R(u,v)\leq0\); thus strict coupling occurs whenever some nonzero component pair satisfies \(R(u+v)<R(u)+R(v)\). Exact decomposability across \((U,V)\) is the boundary case \(\Delta_R\equiv0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Geometry is coupled when combining two structural components changes the regularizer by more than exact additive aggregation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Coupling occurs exactly when there exist \(u\in U\) and \(v\in V\) with \(\Delta_R(u,v)<0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the coupled-geometry leaf and the defect calculation follows from norm subadditivity. The term coupling defect and the classification of every failure of additivity as coupled geometry are uncited and not established as standard terminology, so a supporting source is required.

children.title: Partial-Coupling Regimes
children.top_down_role: Intermediate structures combining separable components with cross-component dependence.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial-Coupling Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative interpolation between exact decomposability and unrestricted cross-component interaction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=U\oplus V\), let \(R\) be a norm, and fix \(\eta\in[0,1]\). The pair \((U,V)\) is in an \(\eta\)-partial-coupling regime when \[0\leq R(u)+R(v)-R(u+v)\leq\eta\bigl(R(u)+R(v)\bigr)\] for every \(u\in U\) and \(v\in V\). Equivalently, \(R(u+v)\geq(1-\eta)(R(u)+R(v))\). The case \(\eta=0\) gives exact decomposability; larger \(\eta\) permits proportionally stronger cancellation between components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial coupling bounds the regularizer’s cross-component cancellation by a fixed fraction of the separate component penalties.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Partial coupling is equivalent to \(R(u+v)\geq(1-\eta)(R(u)+R(v))\) for all component pairs.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind is suitable for a quantitative regime leaf, and the two inequalities are algebraically equivalent. However, this eta-partial-coupling regime is explicitly a proposed quantitative definition with no cited standardization or theoretical source. It cannot be accepted as established mathematical knowledge without such support.

children.title: Regularizer Coupling Choice
children.top_down_role: Selection of separable, grouped, spectral, or coupled regularization structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Regularizer Coupling Choice
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Match regularizer additivity or coupling to the target model’s component interactions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=U\oplus V\) and suppose targets are written \(x=u+v\). If the modeling semantics treat \(u\) and \(v\) independently, a separable choice \(R_{\mathrm{sep}}(x)=R_U(u)+R_V(v)\) is exactly decomposable across \((U,V)\). If admissibility instead constrains joint pairs through a convex atomic set \(\mathcal A\subset U\times V\), use the joint gauge \(R_{\mathrm{joint}}(u+v)=\gamma_{\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A)}(u,v)\). The choice matches the target geometry when its zero coupling defect or nonzero coupling defect agrees with the intended independence or interaction, respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use an additive regularizer for independent components and a joint atomic gauge when the target structure is defined through component interactions.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A\subset U\times V\) is a joint atomic set when coupling is intended.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Choose \(R_{\mathrm{sep}}\) for independent geometry and \(R_{\mathrm{joint}}\) for geometry encoded by joint atoms.

source_refs.locator: 4.3.1 Building the model p. 101

source_witnesses.locator: 4.3.1 Building the model p. 101

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle content kind fits the choice-oriented leaf, but the cited antenna-model section is only indirectly related and does not inspectably support the additive-versus-joint-atomic prescription. The final matching criterion is heuristic and needs a source that specifically treats separable and coupled regularizer design.

children.title: Convex-Surrogate Failure Modes
children.top_down_role: Generic discrepancies between the selected convex gauge and the intended low-complexity model.

children.title: Wrong Atomic Dictionary
children.top_down_role: Bias and nonidentifiability caused by missing or inappropriate atoms.

knowledge_statements.title: Wrong Atomic Dictionary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Missing atoms cause approximation bias; redundant atoms can destroy uniqueness of structural coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D:\mathbb R^m\to X\) map coefficients to combinations of dictionary atoms, and let \(L=\operatorname{range}(D)\). If a target \(x_\star\notin L\), then every dictionary-based estimate \(D\alpha\) satisfies \(\|D\alpha-x_\star\|\geq\operatorname{dist}(x_\star,L)>0\), so exact recovery is impossible. Separately, if \(\ker D\neq\{0\}\) and \(D\alpha=x_\star\), then \(D(\alpha+h)=x_\star\) for every \(h\in\ker D\). Unless the structural criterion selects a unique representative, the same signal has nonunique atomic explanations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dictionary missing the target incurs unavoidable bias, while a dictionary with a nontrivial kernel can give multiple coefficient explanations of one signal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Targets outside \(\operatorname{range}(D)\) are biased, while \(\ker D\neq\{0\}\) permits nonunique coefficient representations.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind matches the topic role. The range-miss bias statement and kernel-based coefficient nonuniqueness are mathematically correct under the stated finite-dimensional coefficient domain, but no source or explicit standard-field rationale is supplied for these nontrivial dictionary failure claims.

\(\ell:S\to\mathcal{L}\) assigns the combinatorial explanation retained by the original model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:

notation.meaning: Barycenter of a finitely supported probability measure on the model set.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: convex hull points retain barycenters but generally not the generating mixtures or their combinatorial labels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex-hull relaxation with labeled structured generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin}}(S)\) denote the finitely supported probability measures on \(S\). Convexification represents each \(z\in\operatorname{conv}(S)\) only through a barycenter \(z=b(\mu)\). Information loss occurs whenever there exist \(\mu,
u\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin}}(S)\) such that \[b(\mu)=b(

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexification loses structural information when distinct mixtures of structured objects have the same barycenter but different combinatorial labels.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexification Information Loss

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the terminal container, and the barycenter criterion is mathematically coherent in the stated finite-dimensional setting. However, the record has no citation supporting the interpretation of convexification as loss of combinatorial-label information, so source verification is required.

children.title: Regularization Shrinkage Bias
children.top_down_role: Magnitude, contrast, or spectral attenuation induced by convex penalties.

assumptions_latex: \(y=x_0\in\mathbb{R}^d\) is observed without noise under the identity map.
\(R:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex, and \(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y-\widehat{x}\in\lambda\partial R(\widehat{x})\), and \(0\notin\partial R(x_0)\) implies \(\widehat{x}\neq x_0\); for \(R(x)=\lVert x\rVert_1\), every surviving coordinate is attenuated by \(\lambda\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: first-order optimality characterizes displacement caused by convex regularization, while coordinatewise attenuation is explicit for the ell-one penalty
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Noiseless identity-observation form of convex penalization bias.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[\widehat{x}=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^d}\left\{\frac12\lVert x-y\rVert_2^2+\lambda R(x)\right\}.\] The estimator is unique and satisfies \[y-\widehat{x}\in\lambda\partial R(\widehat{x}).\] Therefore, if \(0\notin\partial R(x_0)\), then \(\widehat{x}\neq x_0\) despite noiseless data. In the specific case \(R(x)=\lVert x\rVert_1\), \[(\widehat{x})_i=\operatorname{sign}(y_i)(|y_i|-\lambda)_+,\] so every surviving coordinate magnitude is reduced by \(\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive convex penalty can displace a noiseless estimate. For the ell-one penalty specifically, soft thresholding reduces every surviving coordinate magnitude by the regularization level.
knowledge_statements.title: Regularization Shrinkage Bias

children.title: Nonunique Structural Explanations
children.top_down_role: Multiple atomic or component decompositions compatible with the same object.

assumptions_latex: Structural explanations are coefficient vectors measured by \(\lVert\cdot\rVert_1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Distinct minimizers \(c\) and \(d\) certify that the object \(x\) has no uniquely identifiable minimum-cost structural explanation.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: noninjectivity of the synthesis map on minimum-cost coefficient vectors is exactly decomposition nonuniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite atomic synthesis with minimum -cost explanations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in\operatorname{range}(D)\), define its minimum atomic coefficient cost by \[
\gamma_D(x)=\inf\{\lVert a\rVert_1:Da=x\}.
\] A nonunique structural explanation occurs if there are \(c,d\in\mathbb{R}^p\) with \[c\neq d,\qquad Dc=Dd=x,\qquad \lVert c\rVert_1=\lVert d\rVert_1=\gamma_D(x).\] Equivalently, \(h=c-d\) is a nonzero element of \(\ker D\) connecting two minimum-cost feasible coefficient vectors. The synthesized object may therefore be unique while its active atoms, signs, or component allocation remain unidentified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An object has nonunique structure when two distinct minimum-cost coefficient vectors synthesize exactly the same object.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonunique Structural Explanations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind matches the terminal container, and the criterion correctly expresses nonuniqueness among minimum ell-one-cost coefficient explanations. No inspectable citation is supplied for the atomic-synthesis formulation, so the record requires a source.

children.title: Observation-Fidelity Compatibility Boundary
children.top_down_role: Failures caused by incompatibility among model geometry, observation operators, and data-fidelity terms.

children.title: Model–Nullspace Intersections
children.top_down_role: Ambiguity when low-complexity directions lie in the observation nullspace.

assumptions_latex: \(M\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is the admissible low-complexity model set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The map \(x\mapsto Ax\) is injective on \(M\) if and only if \(\ker A\cap(M-M)=\{0\}\); a nontrivial intersection precludes uniform exact recovery on \(M\).

notation.meaning: Difference set of admissible model points.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: injectivity of a linear observation map on a model set is equivalent to trivial intersection of its kernel with the model difference set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Noiseless injectivity boundary for an arbitrary low-complexity model set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(M-M=\{x_1-x_2:x_1,x_2\in M\}\). The observations identify every \(x\in M\) uniquely if and only if \[\ker A\cap(M-M)=\{0\}.\] If this intersection contains a nonzero vector, two distinct points of \(M\) have identical observations, and no estimator can guarantee exact recovery for every point in \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform noiseless identification on the model set is possible exactly when no nonzero difference of two model points lies in the observation nullspace.
knowledge_statements.title: Model–Nullspace Intersections

children.title: Coherent Observation Geometry
children.top_down_role: Measurements aligned with active model directions.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is a closed cone of locally admissible error directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Stable control on \(C\) requires \(\alpha_C(A)>0\); small restricted gain amplifies observation error by at least the reciprocal scale.

notation.meaning: Restricted minimum gain of the observation map.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: restricted minimum singular value on an error cone quantifies alignment between observations and active model directions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restricted-gain formulation of unfavorable observation geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the restricted gain \[
\alpha_C(A)=\inf\{\lVert Ah\rVert_2:h\in C,\ \lVert h\rVert_2=1\}.
\] For every \(h\in C\), one has \(\lVert Ah\rVert_2\geq\alpha_C(A)\lVert h\rVert_2\). Hence, if \(\alpha_C(A)>0\), an admissible error satisfying \(\lVert Ah\rVert_2\leq\delta\) obeys \(\lVert h\rVert_2\leq\delta/\alpha_C(A)\). If \(\alpha_C(A)=0\), unit admissible directions can have arbitrarily small observation norm, so no uniform finite stability constant exists. Coherent alignment is the regime in which \(\alpha_C(A)\) is zero or undesirably small.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Measurements are geometrically unfavorable when they have very small gain along admissible model-error directions, causing severe noise amplification or instability.
knowledge_statements.title: Coherent Observation Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The restricted-gain formulation is mathematically precise and captures the unfavorable observation geometry intended by this failure-boundary leaf. Its stability conclusions follow in the stated finite-dimensional conic setting, but no source or inspectable locator supports the terminology and formulation.

children.title: Noise–Fidelity Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Inappropriate fidelity choices for heavy-tailed, count, impulsive, or adversarial noise.

assumptions_latex: \(n=2k+1\) scalar observations contain at most \(k\) arbitrarily corrupted entries.
Every uncontaminated observation equals a common location \(\theta\in\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Absolute fidelity uniquely returns \(\theta\) under at most \(k\) corruptions, whereas squared fidelity can have arbitrarily large error even under a single corruption.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the sample mean and median provide a sharp contrast between squared and absolute fidelity under impulsive contamination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar impulsive-contamination example contrasting squared and absolute fidelity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(y_1,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb{R}\), where \(n=2k+1\) and at least \(k+1\) entries equal \(\theta\). The absolute-fidelity estimator \[\widehat{t}_1\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\sum_{i=1}^n|y_i-t|\] is uniquely equal to \(\theta\). By contrast, the squared-fidelity estimator is \[\widehat{t}_2=\operatorname*{argmin}_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-t)^2=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n y_i.\] In the case of one corrupted observation equal to \(M\) and \(n-1\) uncontaminated observations equal to \(\theta\), \[|\widehat{t}_2-\theta|=\frac{|M-\theta|}{n},\] which is unbounded as \(|M|\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With fewer than half the observations arbitrarily corrupted, absolute-loss location estimation returns the common uncontaminated value, while one extreme corruption can move the least-squares estimate arbitrarily far.
knowledge_statements.title: Noise–Fidelity Mismatch

children.title: Regularization-Scale Misspecification
children.top_down_role: Underregularized and overregularized model regimes.

assumptions_latex: \(y=x_0+\varepsilon\in\mathbb{R}^d\) is observed under the identity map, where \(x_0\) is the target signal.
For every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,d\}\), the marginal distribution of \(y_i\) is atomless.
The estimator uses the penalty \(\lVert x\rVert_1\) with scale \(\lambda\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At \(\lambda=0\), \(\widehat{x}_0=y\) is dense almost surely, while \(\lambda\geq\lVert y\rVert_\infty\) implies \(\widehat{x}_\lambda=0\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the soft-thresholding solution exhibits exact underregularized and overregularized endpoint regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identity-design ell-one denoising as an exact scale-misspecification boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \[\widehat{x}_\lambda=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^d}\left\{\frac12\lVert x-y\rVert_2^2+\lambda\lVert x\rVert_1\right\}.\] Its coordinates satisfy \[(\widehat{x}_\lambda)_i=S_\lambda(y_i)=\operatorname{sign}(y_i)(|y_i|-\lambda)_+.\] At the underregularized endpoint \(\lambda=0\), \(\widehat{x}_0=y\); because each \(y_i\) has an atomless marginal distribution, \(\widehat{x}_0\) is dense almost surely. At the overregularized endpoint \(\lambda\geq\lVert y\rVert_\infty\), \(\widehat{x}_\lambda=0\), so all observed coordinates are suppressed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For ell-one denoising, zero regularization preserves every continuously distributed observed coordinate almost surely, while a threshold at least as large as the largest observation magnitude sets the entire estimate to zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Regularization-Scale Misspecification
